stories.body:
The fifth plenum comes against a backdrop of years of purges that have had some analysts wondering if the issue is corruption or a lack of loyalty

When Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, he pledged to stamp out corruption all through the ranks of the Communist party. More than a decade later, the pace of investigations has not slowed. Last year, China’s disciplinary authorities opened investigations into more than 1 million people, including more than 100 officials at or above ministerial or provincial level.

As Chinese Communist party (CCP) officials kick off an important meeting this week, discipline – and party loyalty – is high on the agenda. For those who try to read the tea leaves of elite Chinese politics, concern about the apparent lack of discipline is dominating CCP discussions.

The “fifth plenum” began on Monday and is set to focus on “major issues on advancing the party’s full and rigorous self-governance”, according to a Chinese state media. In party-speak, “governance” is a byword for discipline, loyalty and anti-corruption .

As Xi continues to crack down on corruption, the fact that investigations nearly always result in a conviction begs the question over whether targets are truly guilty of corruption, or are they just political rivals to the people in charge.

Kerry Brown, director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London, explained that in Xi’s worldview, which is obsessed with discipline and loyalty, there may not be much difference between the two. “If you’re corrupt, you’re not politically loyal. If you’re politically loyal, you’re not corrupt,” Brown said.

He added that in the CCP system, “corruption is not just material things”, but also “spiritual corruption”, which includes political disloyalty.

Some analysts argue that the reason that the anti-graft drive is so enduring is because corruption is a feature rather than a bug of an authoritarian, top-down political system with a sprawling bureaucracy that governs 1.4 billion people.

Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, said: “Xi has made the party less corrupt and strengthened his control, but he knows that tougher punishment cannot fully resolve the problem of officials putting their own interests ahead of the party’s.

“Xi’s answer is to keep tightening discipline, making anti-corruption a permanent method of governing with no obvious point at which he can declare the job done,” Thomas said.

The job may be never ending, but the plenum is an opportunity to refocus the party’s energy on discipline. The fifth plenum is the fifth of seven gatherings that normally happen in every five-year cycle between CCP congresses. The plenums bring together more than 300 members of the CCP’s Central Committee, the most senior officials in the party hierarchy.

The meeting is particularly significant because it is likely to be the last substantive meeting before next year’s 21st Party Congress, where a new Central Committee will be chosen, and where Xi is expected to be anointed for a fourth term as the head of the CCP.

Eliminating anyone who poses a risk to his authority or to the party’s credibility is a key priority for Xi. And potential threats are everywhere. Nearly 15 years after Xi took office, according to CCP proclamations and a host of recent investigations, the problem is still not stamped out. “It is a deeply ingrained part of [Xi’s] worldview,” said Brown. “Everyone else is corrupt”.

In the past, Xi has warned that the party could “lose its ruling status and inevitably be eliminated by history” if it could not get its house in order. “This is by no means an exaggeration,” he said.

The current focus on party governance comes amid a host of high-profile investigations against senior party and military leaders.

In January, Zhang Youxia , China’s top general and a man second only to Xi in the military hierarchy, was placed under investigation; he was expelled from party last month, having already been removed from the military’s top ruling body, the Central Military Commission (CMC)

A host of other purges means that the CMC, which normally has seven members, has been reduced to just two: Xi and Zhang Shengmin, the CMC’s head of discipline.

Other recent scalps include Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang, and Huang Qifan, the former mayor of Chongqing.

Huang had long been known as the ultimate survivor in Chinese politics because of his connections to the scandals in the early 2010s in which Xi’s political rival, Bo Xilai, the former Party boss for Chongqing, was embroiled in the death of the British businessman Neil Heywood. Bo was ultimately convicted of bribery and embezzlement, for which he is serving a life sentence, but Huang survived. No longer.

Some China analysts have asked whether the recent purges, which have reached the highest echelons of the Party and military ranks, indicate instability in the regime. But Xi likely sees it differently. Corruption investigations demonstrate who is in charge. Plus, Brown added, they are “the most easy and natural tool by which to enforce unity and discipline”.

stories.title: From impulse purchase to pocket studio: The M-Vave FM-1
stories.summary: M-Vave's cheap FM-1 pocket synth has exploded as a community firmware playground.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
M-Vave’s cheap FM-1 pocket synth has exploded as a community firmware playground.

The M-Vave FM-1 is exactly the kind of device I have a weakness for. I may not have an intended use for the frequency-modulation synthesizer, but when a low price meets a high coolness factor, I’m powerless to keep it out of my cart.

Initially billed as a pocket cousin of the famous Yamaha DX7 synthesizer, the FM-1 is a bargain at only $59.72 after fees. At release, it was a cool device that did what it said on the box, but not much else.

But in July, some intrepid tinkerers on Reddit’s r/synthdiy board began reverse-engineering the FM-1’s stock firmware to expand the device’s abilities. By September, custom firmware began appearing. We’re not even through October, and there are already more community firmware projects available to install on the FM-1 than I could ever hope to cover.

I decided to check a few of them out. And just in case you were wondering: Yes, it plays Doom .

Stock firmware and FM1 Open

On October 17, M-Vave announced FM 1 Open, a software package that encourages FM-1 owners to develop custom firmware for the synth-turned-whatever-else-you-can-imagine. Alongside the FM1 Open package came an SDK, a browser-based workbench, and version 15 of the stock firmware, now an open platform you can flash and build on. The unit’s 27 physical piano keys and modest 1.54-inch TFT display lend themselves well to a host of projects, musical or otherwise.

Normally, when an enthusiast community reverse-engineers a closed device, an official patch quickly follows. M-Vave has taken the opposite approach, though. The application source is published under GPLv3 , and the company even includes an in-browser emulator to test custom firmware prior to flashing actual hardware. There’s a caveat, however: The underlying synth engine that powers the stock FM-1 package is still distributed as a closed binary, so it’s the application layer of the stack that’s actually open. I don’t think that diminishes M-Vave’s gesture toward the community, but it’s worth noting.

Proceed at your own risk

Before you rush to AliExpress, be aware that flashing custom firmware comes with risks. The JieLi chip powering the FM-1 keeps firmware in a single flash bank, so an interrupted update can leave the device in a difficult-to-recover state. As long as the flashing process completes without interruption, you should be fine. But nothing is foolproof, and there’s always a risk of bricking a device if something goes wrong.

Flashing will also wipe all information on the device. Before you try to load a new firmware package on the synth, back up your saved projects and settings because they will disappear. I was starting from a blank stock canvas, so there was no real risk.

The unit I received was running stock v14 firmware, and community guides repeatedly warn users to update to the stock v15 firmware before attempting to install custom firmware. Guess who didn’t listen? I blindly assumed that since I’d just received my FM-1, it would be running the latest firmware package (v16 now). I was wrong.

Caught in the excitement, I tried to flash Doom directly onto the v14 firmware package, and the installation failed about 80 percent through. Still, it wrote something. The synth worked, but the device stopped speaking the same language as the installers. Thankfully, M-Vave anticipated careless users like me and thoughtfully included a “force-flash” tool in the FM1 Workbench. It restored my unit to stock v15 in about 10 seconds, saving me a huge headache.

The lesson is simple: Always check your current firmware version.

Custom firmware packages

The development scene around the FM-1 is exploding, and new options are appearing all the time. You can browse the listings to see what you might like to try, and a community tip from the fm1-custom-fw GitHub offers some good advice:

While not an absolute hard rule, there is a prominent community recommendation to avoid flashing one custom firmware directly over another. To minimize bricking risks, some users suggest rolling back to the official stock firmware (v15) via M-VAVE’s official updater first, and only then flashing the next custom firmware build. Alternatively, you can use TransitFM1 —a dedicated lightweight bridge firmware by Quixotic7 designed with crash-guarded boot stubs and stock V15 identity emulation to safely transition between custom builds.

Some other tips I picked up along the way from community discussions and my own mistakes:

Ensure that the FM-1 is fully charged and connected to your PC via USB.

Use a Chromium-based browser for the package installation process. The installers depend on WebUSB and Web MIDI support in the browser, so options like Firefox are out.

Select the FM-1 from a list of available models where applicable.

Use the package’s web-writer to flash the firmware to your FM-1. Do not unplug or power off the unit at any point during this process. Make sure the PC you’re writing the package from isn’t at risk of going to sleep during the write.

Here are some projects to try.

Doom

What better way to measure the value of any electronic device than asking, “will it run Doom ”?

The FM-1 already has several Doom -related projects up and running. Playing on a 240 x 240 display with mini piano keys will never be my preferred way to take down demons with a shotgun, but that doesn’t make it any less cool to see the game running on a $60 synthesizer clone. It’s a novelty, but the clone version played surprisingly well. The short draw distance means enemies occasionally pop out of nowhere, but who doesn’t love a jump scare while demon hunting?

You can explore community Doom options through the fm1-editor directory .

Melodee

While the stock firmware aims to re-create the Yamaha DX7 experience, Melodee takes its cues from the mid-’80s Casio CZ-1, a full-featured synthesizer that uses phase distortion to create a sound modern artists are still chasing. Melodee comes with four engines: a CZ-1 emulator, a DX7-style engine, a percussion engine for the 808s, and my personal favorite, a Commodore 64 SID sound chip emulator.

As a child of the 8-bit era, I’ve always had a soft spot for the amazing soundtracks built around the technological limits of the day. Composing chiptunes always seemed like an interesting hobby, but I never had the right tools. Now, thanks to Melodee, I have a pocketable chiptune keytar I can take anywhere.

Want to re-create that classic Cash Money sound on a $60 budget? The FM-1 now has you covered—this could be your chance to become the next Mannie Fresh.

Felucca

This is where a capable device becomes the deal of the year. Felucca is the foundation for many other community firmware projects, transforming the FM-1 into a true multi-engine synth. The stock firmware lets you select different instruments, but you can play only one at a time. Felucca runs independent instruments simultaneously, letting you create a full-band sound all by yourself.

Felucca includes more than a dozen sound engines, from phase distortion to virtual analog, plus a built-in sampler. Other highlights include a RAW in-browser web editor that makes arranging tracks less painful than working on the FM-1’s tiny screen, and a full multi-track pattern sequencer built into the device. If you want to make music, this is a great place to start.

SLOOP

SLOOP is the FM-1’s groovebox solution. Cards on the table: Before writing this article, I wasn’t familiar with what a groovebox was. In a nutshell, it’s a self-contained music studio that can be operated without a PC. SLOOP turns the FM-1 from an instrument you play into one you compose with. You program drums and bass on a grid, chain loops together, and let the machine keep the beat going while you layer other sounds on top.

SLOOP adds drum machines and synth layers to the FM-1, running on Felucca’s sound engines. The result is a legitimate eight-track, battery-powered beat maker that fits in your pocket. Unlike Felucca, SLOOP is designed more for live performance, letting you build and stack layers of sound as you go. I didn’t always fully understand how I arrived at the results I produced in SLOOP, but I was having too much fun to care.

In the studio

After exploring some of the available custom firmware packages, I decided to take my own advice and try Felucca as a starting point for actual recording. I connected the FM-1 to my PC using the same USB connection I’d previously used for flashing. Audacity recognized Felucca immediately, and I was able to select it as a recording device. From there, I could select any instrument or effect on the device and record it live over USB to Audacity tracks.

That’s all well and good if you’re sitting at a desk with a PC, but what if inspiration strikes while you’re out and about? That’s where Felucca’s self-contained recording process shines.

Creating music entirely on the FM-1 was more intuitive than I expected. Once I pulled up the Felucca controls cheat sheet , the process was smooth: use the Algorithm knob to switch between recording tracks and Presets to switch instruments. From there, I could build and layer my creation track by track.

I put together a four-track beat loop after about 15 minutes of fiddling with the firmware. I just felt my way around in the dark, auditioning sounds and slipping them in wherever I thought they fit. It was about as simplistic as it gets, but with some time and practice, I think I could churn out something worthwhile. If it was this straightforward for me, just imagine what someone with actual musical talent could achieve.

I’ll admit that my fingers were occasionally too big for the task. The FM1’s soft-touch keys feel great, but my index finger sometimes slipped off the intended note and onto an adjacent key. It’s not a dealbreaker, but there were a few times I had to retry a part due to hitting a wrong note.

Since there doesn’t appear to be an on-device export function, transferring the track to my PC was as simple as opening Audacity and hitting record while playing a beat on the FM-1. I retained live control throughout recording, too. Toward the end of the sample below, you can hear me fading out the audio by turning down the master volume knob. The same approach would let you weave any number of live modulations into a recording. You can hear my modest attempt at a quick beat below.

Final thoughts

The FM-1 is the type of technology I love. I’m the furthest thing from a professional musician, but the price is low enough and the device is versatile enough that I can play around without feeling guilty about a $1,500 synth setup gathering dust in the corner.

My 10-year-old has been taking piano lessons for a few years now and has clearly inherited my urge to tinker with tech. The FM-1 could be the perfect holiday gift he never knew he needed. I’ll probably order another one for him since I still want to play with mine. At this price, I don’t have to sweat it. M-Vave didn’t send this unit for review; checkout curiosity just got the better of me. I’ve since ordered the company’s SMC-PAD sampler, too, but that’s another article for another day. Would I buy the FM-1 again tomorrow? In a beat.

stories.title: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing
stories.summary: The company will be the first true artificial intelligence company to go public as tech firms continue to invest heavily in AI.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 26 October 2026, 13:27 GMT

Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.

The company behind AI chatbot Claude revealed losses of more than $80.7bn (£60.5bn) in the first half of the year, but said it had $112.4bn in cash or equivalents, and generated revenues of $16.3bn over the same period.

The number of shares to be released, their price range, and a date for the listing have not been disclosed.

Anthropic's valuation when it goes public has been expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which this summer was the biggest-ever stock listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion.

In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.

It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".

Anthropic will be the first true AI company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.

It said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT.

Anthropic, which was founded just five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five other co-founders, announced its intention to go public in June.

Its most significant rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit, saying it, too, intended to go public. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.

After the companies had decided on such plans, a wave of cyber-security and other types of technological breaches occurred involving their AI agents, or AI bots that are designed to operate somewhat autonomously.

Current and former staff of both companies also gained public attention with new warnings that AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect the whole of humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.

'Bold but sane'

In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.

In its financial filings, Anthropic detailed losses that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".

"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.

Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".

Tech companies have been heavily investing in costly AI infrastructure and tools, like data centres and the informational models that underly all AI technology, pouring more than $1tn into the efforts over the last year alone.

stories.summary: Ninety-plus Labour MPs warn civil service lacks skills to drive growth where it is needed and plan should be steered by Louise Haigh from Manchester Business live – latest updates Andy Burnham’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain is doomed to fail unless it is driven decisively from his new No 10 North outpost in Manchester, a group of more than 90 backbench Labour MPs have said. stories.body:
Ninety-plus Labour MPs warn civil service lacks skills to drive growth where it is needed and plan should be steered by Louise Haigh from Manchester

Business live – latest updates

Andy Burnham’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain is doomed to fail unless it is driven decisively from his new No 10 North outpost in Manchester, a group of more than 90 backbench Labour MPs have said.

The PM has suggested that rebuilding the UK’s industrial capacity will be central to meeting his pledge to bring “good growth in every postcode” .

John Healey, who will deliver his first budget as chancellor on Wednesday, used his speech at Labour’s conference last month to promise a “new age of industrialisation”.

However, in a briefing paper seen by the Guardian, the backbenchers warn that decades of deindustrialisation and deregulation mean the government no longer has the detailed understanding of industry needed to make such a plan work.

“The state has lost capacity and has acquired a worrying set of behaviours which will inhibit reindustrialisation. The state has become less knowledgable about the state of the economy and our businesses, unable to comprehensively plan and slow to make decisions,” the paper says.

The MPs are calling on Burnham to pass a new Reindustrialisation Act, to set clear targets for creating jobs by rebuilding the country’s manufacturing capacity, and to ensure ministers are held to account against them. “If we do not plan for reindustrialisation, we cannot achieve it,” the group argues.

The briefing paper urges the PM to give the job of overseeing reindustrialisation to the first secretary of state, Louise Haigh, and base it at No 10 North, the Manchester outpost he established in July, which has already taken on some responsibility for growth policy .

And the paper argues that the National Wealth Fund – the arm’s length body that invests in promising businesses – should be transformed into a Reindustrialisation Development Corporation, whose primary job is to provide capital for rebuilding UK industry.

Andy MacNae, the MP for Rossendale and Darwen, who chairs the group, said: “I’ve got absolutely no doubt about Andy or John’s commitment to this, but there is a kind of inertia in government, within the civil service, within economic orthodoxy, that still says that growth policy is about cities – it’s about the places that are already doing well.”

Instead, he said, reindustrialisation must be about “delivering jobs to the places that need them most.” He added: “It’s about making things again, and it’s about making the things that give us national resilience in a turbulent world.”

He cited the government’s recent decision to nationalise British Steel , adding that reindustrialisation involved policies across government, from procurement to education.

after newsletter promotion

Steve Yemm, the MP for the former mining constituency of Mansfield, said: “Countries around the world are reindustrialising, yet too many in Whitehall still treat industrial policy as dangerous nostalgia. We need the prime minister’s full backing to challenge those outdated assumptions.”

A third member of the group, Lorraine Beavers, the MP for Blackpool North and Fleetwood, said she was enthusiastic about the promise of reindustrialisation for constituencies like hers, but said: “If I have learned anything since becoming an MP two years ago, it’s that Whitehall doesn’t fix a problem unless it is told to.”

In its industrial strategy , published while Keir Starmer was prime minister, Labour identified eight sectors ripe for growth, including advanced manufacturing, clean energy and defence.

In his conference speech, to which Healey had invited a young apprentice who had worked on building a new Mersey ferry, the chancellor said Labour would “get Britain growing. With hope for our young people. With good work, good jobs and a new age of industrialisation.”

stories.title: Burnham leaves door open to referendum on EU free movement
stories.summary: The PM says he wants to start a conversation about potential options for the UK's future relationship with the EU.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 26 October 2026, 12:16 GMT

The prime minister has left the door open to a potential referendum on freedom of movement with the European Union.

Asked by broadcasters if he could introduce free movement without a referendum, Andy Burnham said "no", but sources told the BBC no decision on that has been made.

The PM added that he would "never move ahead of the British public when it comes to Brexit".

Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election but says he wants start a conversation about potential options, with these expected to be set out around the time of the EU summit next month.

Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.

The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.

The prime minister is thought to be against the idea of leaping quickly to a return to freedom of movement.

Sources indicated no firm decision had been made on whether free movement would need to be rubber-stamped by a referendum.

Burnham is said to believe that a conversation about the UK's future relationship with Brussels needs to happen first.

Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about freedom of movement allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.

Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement Published 5 hours ago

Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham Published 30 September

Burnham has said he is committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

The PM has stressed any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

However, he has suggested potential options for the future could range from no changes to the UK-EU relationship, to rejoining the EU customs union, the single market or a new in-out referendum on full EU membership.

In an interview with the Sunday Times , external , Burnham said he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and the EU.

The PM argued that the type of migration had changed since Brexit, with more foreigners moving permanently.

In contrast, he suggested that when the UK was a member of the EU, migration was "generally younger people", who would spend a few years in the country before returning home.

However, Burnham added: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."

The Schengen Agreement, which the UK was not part of when it was in the EU, allows passport-free travel across member countries.

The UK was able to keep the pound when it was an EU member, but the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the Euro.

Burnham has argued that since Brexit, the UK has lost immigration control the country previously had.

"For instance, the small boats crisis has arisen in the last 10 years because we lost that returns agreement when people came here that we could work with other countries to return them," he told broadcasters.

The Conservatives and Reform UK both oppose a return to free movement with the EU.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch argued most people who voted for Brexit did so because they did not want free movement, while Reform leader Nigel Farage said such a move would be "a total betrayal of Brexit Britain".

However, the Liberal Democrats have argued that allowing freedom of movement would help economic growth.

stories.title: ‘We don’t have inflation’? Five charts show the US economic reality of Trump’s second term so far

stories.body:
As the US midterm elections approach, we take a look at data to see a true picture of the US economy under Trump

With the midterm elections fast approaching, many Americans have the economy on their minds.

US voters are exhausted by years of higher prices. Donald Trump won the presidency in 2024 on promises to lower inflation and undo the damage he said the Biden administration had inflicted on the economy.

In Trump’s view, his plan is working. At a recent rally in Montana, Trump boasted about the current economy, framing it as a booming time for Americans. “We’re richer now,” he said. “We don’t have inflation.”

Economic data paints a different picture. Inflation , especially gas prices, have soared over the last year. The job market has been in stasis, and higher interest rates have meant it’s more expensive for Americans to borrow money for loans and mortgages.

These fluctuations have a concrete impact on the lives of Americans. A recent Harris poll for the Guardian found that a majority of Americans, including some Republicans, disagree. Nearly two-thirds said they believe the country is experiencing a recession, and many said higher prices have been a pain point. Americans are reporting having trouble saving, and a third polled said one surprise bill could sink them financially.

Here’s what the data shows us about Trump’s second term so far.

Inflation

The rate of price increases has dramatically cooled since its peak in 2022, when the pandemic’s economic stimulus packages found their way into consumer prices. Inflation peaked at 9.1%, a 40-year high, in June 2022.

In January 2025, the month when Trump started his second term, inflation was down to 3%. By April 2025, it would be 2.3% – the lowest rate since 2021.

That’s when things start to get bumpy. After Trump placed tariffs on nearly everything that the US imports, inflation started to heat up again, climbing back up to 3% in September 2025. After many of his tariffs were paused and eventually found to be illegal, prices started going down again. In January and February 2026, inflation was back down to 2.4%.

The Iran war, specifically its impact on oil prices, has brought inflation back up to levels not seen since 2023. In May, inflation reached 4.2% and has hovered above 3.4% since.

It’s been nearly six years since Americans has seen inflation at a manageable 2% level. Price increases build up over time and can put a squeeze on budgets, which is why it’s such a sensitive point for voters during a crucial election.

Gas prices

In the Guardian’s recent poll with the Harris Poll, gas prices were the most common pain point for Americans, with 83% saying they’re making a dent in their current finances.

Soon after the war in Iran began, the strait of Hormuz, a key route that a fifth of the world’s oil typically passes through, was blocked off. Its closure has pushed up prices all around the world. Though the US itself is a major oil producer, prices have still surged since the war. The average price of gas was $4.32 per gallon in mid-October, according to AAA, nearly $1.30 a gallon higher than a year ago.

Even for an oil-producing state like Texas, a gallon of gas is $3.81 compared with $2.64 a year ago. Meanwhile, drivers in California, a state that imports much of its gas from overseas, are paying $6.21 per gallon.

Monthly job figures

The labor market is another metric used to measure the health of the economy, and while the US job market has seen some growth since Trump took office again, figures have fluctuated over the last year. In 2025, altogether 181,000 new jobs were added to the economy, compared with 2.2m jobs in 2024.

Employers have been dealing with a mixed landscape for hiring: harsher immigration policies, uncertainty from tariffs and higher prices for supplies have all meant slow job growth. The unemployment rate has remained low, though, at just over 4%. Economists call this a “low-hire, low-fire” economy, in which employers are neither hiring or laying off workers.

S&P 500

Though many Americans report struggling in today’s economy, a small handful have never been wealthier. The stock market has continued to soar since Trump took office, recovering from dips seen during his initial tariff announcement and the early days of the Iran war.

Economists largely see AI investment as the leading factor in the stock market’s acceleration. Tech companies are spending billions of dollars investing in datacenters and for chips that are needed to power AI.

While many Americans are invested in the stock market through their retirement and pension funds, this growth has really been a boon for the top 1% wealthiest Americans, who own nearly half of the stock market investments.

Economists say higher prices paired with an exuberant stock market has led to a K-shaped economy , where the wealthier have never felt richer while everyday Americans continue to deal with tightened budgets from high prices.

Interest rates

Interest rates are often not as noticeable to consumers as gas or grocery prices, which they come across every day. The impact that higher interest rates have on the economy takes longer to appear and runs deep. Interest rates shape how much Americans pay to borrow money – to run their businesses, pay off car loans and buy their homes.

For the Federal Reserve, shifting interest rates is the tool it uses to balance the economy. Raising rates can cool the economy, bringing prices down, though at the risk of hurting the job market. Lowering rates can stimulate the economy at the risk of leading to more inflation.

When Trump entered office in January 2025, the Fed was in the middle of a series of interest rate reductions. Officials said they were seeing inflation cooling and slower growth in the labor market. Interest rates were at a range of 4.25% to 4.5% – 1% lower than they were a year ago.

Uncertainty around Trump’s new tariffs would ultimately lead officials to pause the reduction, though the president was still demanding lower rates. As tariffs proved to have less of a long-term effect on prices, the Fed started lowering rates again in fall 2025.

For months, the Fed held off on changing rates as the economic impacts of the war of Iran bore out. But in September, the Fed hiked rates for the first time since 2023, by a quarter point. The Trump-appointed Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, said that “inflation is too high and has been for too long”.

Higher interest rates have already had an impact on mortgage rates, which had dipped down to below 6% (for a 30-year mortgage) for the first time since 2022, in February, but are now up past 7%.

Faced with a stagnant jobs market, many are spurning children or pets in favour of ‘raising bricks’

Young adults in China looking for a cheaper, low-maintenance alternative to having children or pets have found an answer: raising bricks.

Bricks may not be as cuddly as cats or as life-affirming as human offspring, but they also cost next to nothing. “No cats, no dating, I started raising a brick,” wrote one brick parent on social media.

Raising “brick babies” is easier than caring for house plants, involving spraying them with water a few times a day then waiting for moss spores already present in the atmosphere to attach themselves and grow. One Chinese media article described the bricks as being “practically immortal”. “If you forget to water them, the moss goes dormant. If you remember to water them again, the greenery returns.”

A hashtag related to the trend has attracted more than 5m views on the Chinese social media platform Weibo.

Chinese commentators have linked the trend to young people looking for low-effort routes to finding meaning in life. One brick “parent” told Chinese media the hobby created “a sense of accomplishment no less than completing a long-term project”.

One user on Xiaohongshu, an Instagram-like platform, also known as Rednote, posted a picture of their rusty-coloured brick, saying “no output required, no KPIs to hit, no need to beg it to bloom [and] no comparing its growth with others”.

Another user wrote: “My friends asked if I’d lost my mind. I said no, I’m just starting to raise a brick.

“A brick gives me a sense of certainty that feels way more grounded than a lot of relationships. Psychologists call this ‘zero-energy emotional companionship.’ It fulfils your need for company without demanding any obligation to give love in return.”

Young people in China are increasingly shunning the traditional expectations of society, such as having children and working long hours in strenuous jobs, assuming they can find one in the first place. Nearly one in five 16- to 24-year-olds, excluding students, are unemployed , according to official statistics. Some estimates put the unemployment rate much higher.

China’s birthrate is in decline and fell to a record low last year. Faced with a sluggish job market after years of intensely competitive studying, many young people are choosing to shun the rat race and opt instead for “ lying flat ” – pursuing a low-effort, low-stress lifestyle; one well-suited to raising bricks.

The trend has become so popular that Chinese media have started to warn about the health risks.

Cultivating moss could lead to the spread of mould, with some “brick parents” reportedly complaining of itchy eyes and runny noses. Xuedong Li, a retired professor of moss from Beijing’s Capital Normal University, urged people to keep their bricks in an enclosed environment. “It is best to wear disposable gloves and a mask during handling to reduce spore inhalation and skin contact,” Li told Chinese media.

stories.title: Funding set to double for plan to get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas
stories.summary: Burnham made ending rough sleeping his first pledge when entering Downing Street in July.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The pledge was one of Burnham's key early announcements after becoming prime minister in July

Published 25 October 2026

Funding is set to double to support a pledge by the prime minister to give every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas.

Ending rough sleeping was one of Andy Burnham's first promises when he entered Downing Street, announcing a £442m package to provide emergency accommodation and practical support.

Ahead of the first Rough Sleeping Summit at Downing Street on Monday, No 10 has indicated a further £432m will be added to the initiative in Wednesday's Budget.

Shadow housing secretary Katie Lam said rough sleeping had hit "record highs under Labour" and criticised Burnham for failing to end rough sleeping when he was the Mayor of Greater Manchester.

The most recent official figures estimated there were 4,793 people sleeping rough , external on a single night in autumn 2025 in England.

The government's commitment is that every rough sleeper will either be able to physically move into accommodation by Christmas or will have been offered support as a way to prevent them sleeping rough.

Money being added to the pot this week will extend support beyond March 2027 to the end of this Parliament, taking total investment to £874m.

Burnham told ITV's Good Morning Britain he was confident it could be done, saying: "I have this strong feeling about putting the right standards at the heart of the country again and we can't get to a position where we just become used to walking past people sleeping rough: it's about care for people."

He added: "In the end, actually, it's cheaper to do that than to leave people sleeping rough going in and out of A&E, that's not good for anybody."

As Mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham pledged to end rough sleeping in in the region by 2020, setting up the Bed Every Night scheme, which now provides more than 600 beds per night for people who might otherwise be on the streets.

When he was elected in 2017 government figures showed there were 268 rough sleepers across Greater Manchester, and by 2020 that figure had more than halved to 125 - meaning Burnham missed his target.

The numbers fell further to 90 in 2021, but the figures rose each year after that, reaching 197 by 2025.

Asked about his previous attempts to end rough sleeping in Manchester during his time as mayor of the region, he said: "I bring the learning from that to this.

"The reason why the figures went back up is because we were the only place that was offering a bed every night, so people came to Greater Manchester knowing that we were providing a higher level of support...I realised that it's only if everywhere does it at the same level that you can actually end rough sleeping."

The Conservatives' Lam said: "Burnham is throwing another £432m at a problem he failed to solve in Greater Manchester."

Across England, government figures show the number of people sleeping rough is at its highest level since records began in 2010.

Lam said: "Under Labour, rough sleeping has hit record highs – yet their answer is always more taxpayers' money and more empty promises.

"Healey must use his Budget this week to cut taxes for working people, get the ballooning benefits bill under control, and stop pushing up energy prices.

"Instead of piling more costs onto hard-working people, Healey must focus on easing the cost of living and delivering real value for taxpayers' money."

Burnham unveils plan to get rough sleepers off streets for Christmas Published 19 August

Key takeaways as Andy Burnham becomes PM Published 20 July

Burnham pledges to end rough sleeping in first speech as prime minister Published 20 July

More than 30 organisations have pledged support for Burnham's plan with new partnerships, including commercial businesses and charities who attended Monday's summit.

Initial funding has seen specialist outreach teams and new bed spaces operating in Coventry, with further provision being rolled out in places including Plymouth and Camden in north London over the coming weeks.

The National Housing Federation will now work with housing associations to identify at least 2,000 potential homes and bed spaces, including empty properties that could be brought back into use.

However, questions remain about whether the scale of accommodation currently identified will be sufficient. It is not yet clear how many of the 2,000 homes and bedspaces represent self-contained units and how many could accommodate multiple people.

While homelessness organisations have welcomed the government's focus on rough sleeping, many have urged ministers to go further in the Budget.

Leaders from 40 organisations across the housing and homelessness sector signed an open letter last week calling on the government to restore Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rates so they continue to reflect local rents, arguing this would help prevent homelessness in the first place and reduce reliance on temporary accommodation.

The Resolution Foundation estimates that more than 1.1 million low income renters now face shortfalls between their housing benefit and their actual rent, with the gap expected to reach a record high this October.

It argues that relinking LHA to local rents would primarily benefit struggling tenants and help keep more people in their homes.

Housing organisations say that while helping people already sleeping rough is essential, preventing people from becoming homeless in the first place will be critical if the government's longer-term ambition is to succeed.

stories.title: Steinmeier in China: A major state visit in uncertain times
stories.summary: President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is traveling to China on a state visit in a period of political and economic uncertainty. Germany is seeking alternative partners in the region, but also wants good ties with Beijing.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is traveling to China on a state visit in a period of political and economic uncertainty. Germany is seeking alternative partners in the region, but also wants good ties with Beijing.

Eight years have passed since Frank-Walter Steinmeier's last trip to China . Since then, the relationship between China and Europe has changed significantly. The German president plans to spend several days touring China before concluding his visit in Beijing, where he will meet with China's leaders.

His visit comes just as the Chinese Communist Party's Central Committee is convening for its plenary session, a major annual event that foreign dignitaries usually avoid when timing their visits.

The focus of the president's five-day trip will be "Germany's diverse and complex relations with China, as well as the challenges involved," his office said in a statement. In addition to sites of cultural exchange, the itinerary will also include a visit to a Volkswagen plant in Hefei.

A diplomatic balancing act

The automotive industry, in particular, illustrates the dilemma facing Germany's China policy. China is one of the most important markets for German automotive and machinery manufacturers, as well as for the chemical industry. At the same time, state-supported overcapacity in China is putting pressure on European manufacturers.

Not only that. Germany and Europe are dependent on China for raw materials and technologies, which means they are increasingly seeking out alternative partnerships.

Steinmeier was once an advocate of the policy of "change through trade" — the idea that other countries could be persuaded to become more democratic with the leverage of global trade — which has few adherents left in Germany today.

Now he must now pursue a tougher European line in Beijing. Caught between partnership and competition, Europe leaders recently managed to reach an agreement: Imports of plug-in hybrid vehicles from China are to be scaled back.

"That was a concrete step, but it can only be the beginning," said Michael Laha, an expert on China at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) in Berlin.

Why big automakers are losing China

Chancellor and president both in Asia

Coinciding with Steinmeier's state visit to China, Chancellor Friedrich Merz is traveling to the Indo-Pacific with business representatives. His visit to Japan, Singapore and South Korea will focus on competitiveness, technological upheavals, defense cooperation and critical raw materials. Merz is visiting companies and attending important regional economic conferences in Tokyo and Seoul.

The dual trips are Berlin's attempt to send a twofold message: While the chancellor is "deliberately strengthening Germany's partnerships in the Indo-Pacific at a time of global upheaval," according to Laha, the president is seeking dialogue with Beijing at a time when Germany and Europe are recalibrating their relationship with China.

"This joint trip sends a very well-coordinated message to the Chinese that we remain committed to the partnership but at the same time are taking steps to reduce risk," said Laha, before adding that this is a difficult balancing act that also allows China to save face.

Little room for human rights

While Merz will be accompanied by a large economic delegation, Steinmeier will be traveling to China with representatives from German culture, politics, and academia. Mikko Huotari, director of the China Institute MERICS, is also expected to be part of the delegation — even though Beijing has imposed sanctions on the institute. "The fact that he is coming along sends a clear message to the Chinese side that we do not approve of the sanctions," said Laha.

In 2021, the EU imposed sanctions against several Chinese party and regional officials, as well as an organization accused of serious human rights violations and oppressing the Uyghur minority. It was the first time such sanctions had been imposed on China since the Tiananmen Square massacre in 1989, and Beijing did not take kindly to them:

. In response, the Chinese government imposed entry bans and other sanctions against European politicians, scholars, and institutions, including MERICS.

Laha did not expect human rights to play a major role in the German president's trip. Steinmeier is considered a pragmatist when it comes to China policy. As foreign minister, he distanced himself from his predecessor Joschka Fischer, a critic of China, and even criticized Chancellor Angela Merkel when she hosted the Dalai Lama.

China should assume international responsibility

On the subject of Ukraine, Steinmeier is likely to be more direct and raise the issue of China's role in the conflict. "Beijing is clearly on Moscow's side," said Laha. In Berlin, however, officials are convinced that China can do more to persuade Russia to engage in serious negotiations and find a solution to the conflict.

Steinmeier may make this clear in his speech at Peking University on Thursday. Germany has "long viewed China's emergence with respect and goodwill," read a statement from the president's office. Today, however, the focus is less on China's continued rise and more on how it uses its growing power.

"If the president points out that Russia used its power to attack a sovereign state, he could be alluding to another regional connection: Taiwan ," said Laha. That could be seen as an appeal to Beijing to assume more responsibility for the regional and international order.

To conclude his visit, Steinmeier will meet with China's leadership in Beijing. Talks are planned with President Xi Jinping, whom he has known for nearly two decades, as well as with Premier Li Qiang and the chairman of the National People's Congress, Zhao Leji.

The trip marks the culmination of Steinmeier's focus on Asia during his second term in office. Since then, he has deliberately sought to forge close ties with partners in the region and has advocated for greater diversification. Now China – Germany's most important and most challenging partner – will come to its own conclusion.

stories.title: Germany news: Union slams Audi CEO for joining Trump at campaign rally, while Chancellor Merz and President Steinmeier embark on separate Asia tours
stories.summary: Audi's boss is facing a backlash in Germany after appearing alongside Donald Trump at a campaign rally. Meanwhile, Germany's chancellor and president are heading to Asia on separate diplomatic missions. DW has more.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Audi's boss is facing a backlash in Germany after appearing alongside Donald Trump at a campaign rally. Meanwhile, Germany's chancellor and president are heading to Asia on separate diplomatic missions. DW has more.

What you need to know

Germany's IG Metall union chief calls Audi CEO Gernot Döllner's appearance alongside Donald Trump "deeply embarrassing"

The union says Döllner breached Audi's political neutrality rules

Chancellor Friedrich Merz is visiting Singapore, Japan and South Korea

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is heading to China

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Monday, October 26, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Cruise captain investigated after Bremerhaven collision

German police are investigating the captain of the Mein Schiff 3 cruise liner after it collided with two container ships in Bremerhaven, forcing the cancellation of a 20-day voyage to the Canary Islands .

Police opened administrative offense proceedings to establish whether the captain breached his duty of care. They have not specified the suspected lapse.

A gust of wind pushed the liner toward the container ships as tugboats assisted its departure on Sunday evening, police said. All three vessels were damaged, but none took on water and nobody was injured.

The cruise ship had 2,428 passengers and 922 crew members on board.

Police estimate damage running into the millions. The collision tore open a section of the larger container ship's port side, while photographs showed damage to the liner's lifeboats and bridge.

All three ships have been barred from leaving port pending checks. Tui Cruises said it was unclear whether further scheduled voyages would be affected.

Union chief condemns Audi boss's Trump rally appearance

Germany's IG Metall union chief Christiane Benner has sharply criticized Audi CEO Gernot Döllner for appearing onstage at a campaign rally with US President Donald Trump.

Benner called the appearance "deeply embarrassing, politically unacceptable" and unworthy of Audi and its employees. She also accused Döllner of breaching the company's political neutrality rules.

Audi's code of conduct, published in April and signed by Döllner, bars public appearances with parties or politicians standing for election, and sponsorship of their events, during the three months before a vote.

Trump announced plans for an Audi factory in Georgia at Saturday's rally, with Döllner alongside him. The plant would produce around 200,000 vehicles annually, mainly large SUVs.

Benner stressed that the project still required approval, with the final decision "rightly and importantly" resting with Volkswagen's supervisory board, "with the full picture in mind."

She said employee representatives wanted safeguards for German sites alongside a clear North American strategy for Volkswagen and Audi. While acknowledging the US market's importance, she said IG Metall's priority was employment prospects in Germany.

READ — Harry Kane seen as Ballon d'Or frontrunner after record Bayern season

Bayern Munich and England striker Harry Kane could break a series of English and German droughts in London tonight at the Ballon d'Or award ceremony.

Most bookmakers consider him the favorite among the 30 nominees, even amid stiff competition from the likes of World Cup winner Lamine Yamal and French superstar Kylian Mbappe.

Kane would be the first English winner of world football's most prestigious individual award since Michael Owen in 2001.

The Bayern star would be the first Bundesliga player to win since Matthias Sammer in 1996, and the first Bayern Munich player since Karl-Heinz Rummenigge in 1981.

The 33-year-old's record-setting 73-goal season for Bayern and England is Exhibit A when making the case for him, but there's more to it even than that.

Matt Pearson on our sports desk explores the arguments for and against in depth here .

READ — Merz heads to Asia amid security and trade concerns

Chancellor Friedrich Merz is visiting Singapore, Japan and South Korea as Germany seeks stronger partnerships amid security threats and uncertainty over global supply chains.

Read more about this story here .

READ — Steinmeier visits China in uncertain times

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is traveling to China on a state visit in a period of political and economic uncertainty.

Germany is seeking alternative partners in the region, but also wants good ties with Beijing.

Read DW's full report on President Steinmeier's trip to China .

Berlin Left leader says Dobrindt plan is unconstitutional

Berlin Left Party leader Elif Eralp has called Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt's proposal to restrict the socialization of property unconstitutional.

"You cannot use a federal law to make impossible what the Basic Law provides for and what Berliners voted for," Eralp told public broadcaster ZDF on Monday. She said the proposal had nothing to do with protecting investment and was aimed at Berlin's tenants.

Under Dobrindt’s plan, a state government would have to prove that socialization was unavoidable and that it had exhausted all alternatives, including investment in and support for new housing. Compensation would have to be paid immediately in cash and based on the property’s market value, determined by an expert assessment.

Eralp said that setting compensation at market value could make socialization impossible. "It is an attempt to prevent socialization," she said.

Eralp could become Berlin's first governing mayor from the Left Party . After winning the state election, her party is negotiating a coalition with the Greens and the Social Democrats. The parties plan to target private housing companies with more than 10,000 apartments and estimate compensation would cost €16 billion (about $18 billion), likely below the properties’ market value.

Why Germany's political center is losing ground

State premier criticizes Audi boss's Trump appearance

Lower Saxony premier Olaf Lies has criticized Audi CEO Gernot Döllner's appearance alongside US President Donald Trump at a campaign rally, saying he had become part of a political spectacle.

"A campaign rally cannot be the right place to announce an investment of this magnitude," said Lies, whose state is Volkswagen's second-largest shareholder.

Trump announced plans for an Audi factory in Georgia at Saturday's rally, with Döllner onstage alongside him.

"This appearance has caused consternation among employees who are worried about their jobs here, and far beyond. I can fully understand that — I feel the same way," Lies said.

His comments follow criticism from IG Metall union chief Christiane Benner, who accused Döllner of breaching Audi's political neutrality rules.

German weightlifters question Russia's 2030 Worlds award

Germany's weightlifting federation says it will critically examine the decision to award the 2030 world championships to Moscow, while stopping short of an outright condemnation.

The International Weightlifting Federation becomes the first Olympic sports federation to award Russia a global sporting event since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The German Weightlifting Federation said it would assess the decision's political, ethical and international implications.

"The complexity of the situation must not mean that fundamental questions and the necessary critical examination of this decision are neglected," it told the SID sports news agency.

The championships will also serve as a qualifying event for the 2032 Olympics, adding to the significance of the decision.

Track worker killed after ICE train hits two in Essen

A track worker has died and another has been seriously injured after an ICE high-speed train struck them in the western German city of Essen.

The two were among six workers on a section of Deutsche Bahn track late on Sunday evening, the fire service said.

Emergency crews pronounced one worker dead at the scene. The injured colleague was lifted from the tracks to street level using a fire engine's aerial ladder and taken to hospital.

Police are investigating the cause of the accident.

The line between Gelsenkirchen's main station and Essen-Altenessen remained closed in the morning as cleanup work continued. The train had been removed, a railway spokesperson said.

Long-distance services were being diverted between Gelsenkirchen and Duisburg. Regional passengers were advised to check alternative routes.

German cruise ship cancels voyage after port collision

German cruise operator Tui Cruises has canceled a 20-day voyage to the Canary Islands after its cruise ship "Mein Schiff 3" collided with two container vessels in the northern port of Bremerhaven .

Tugboats were helping the nearly fully booked cruise ship, carrying 2,428 passengers and 922 crew members, leave port on Sunday evening when a gust of wind pushed it toward two moored container ships, police said.

All three vessels sustained damage. One container ship suffered extensive damage to its port side, with several meters of its hull torn open above the waterline. The cruise ship also suffered significant damage, including to its lifeboats and bridge.

There were no injuries or water ingress on any of the vessels. All three ships have been temporarily prohibited from leaving port while investigations continue.

Tui Cruises said technical experts had inspected the vessel and determined that repairs at a shipyard were necessary, forcing the cancellation of the planned voyage.

The company described the cancellation as "the only responsible decision," stressing that passenger and crew safety remained its highest priority.

Merz and Steinmeier head to Asia on separate trips

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and President Frank-Walter Steinmeier are departing on separate Asian tours to strengthen economic and diplomatic ties.

Merz will visit Singapore , Japan and South Korea on his longest overseas trip since taking office, accompanied by a high-level business delegation. He is seeking to broaden Germany's partnerships and reduce dependence on individual countries.

In Singapore, he will hold political talks and deliver a major foreign policy speech before traveling to Japan. In South Korea, he will attend an Asia-Pacific business conference and visit the demilitarized zone separating North and South Korea.

Steinmeier will make his second state visit to China , pressing for fairer trade relations and action to address economic imbalances, according to his office.

He is expected to speak at Peking University on Thursday and meet President Xi Jinping and Premier Li Qiang on Friday.

Steinmeier also wants China to take greater international responsibility, including using its close ties with Moscow to help end Russia's war against Ukraine.

Facebook, Wordpress, Wikipedia, Etsy, and other major sites all use or were originally built on PHP. It is a long-established mainstay of web development. stories.title: Computer Security Is About to Get a Lot Worse, Here’s What You Can Do
stories.summary: It is a commonly held truth among computer geeks that there is no such thing as bug free software, or a secure computer. Any piece of software that anyone actually uses will have a security vulnerability somewhere in the code . The more complex that software is, the more likely there will be a vulnerability. Fortunately for everyone, finding severe vulnerabilities was generally considered an expensive and difficult task requiring years of training and deep knowledge of how computers and software worked. Until recently there was a steady background hum of vulnerabilities being found and patched, with major vulnerabilities that could cripple the entire internet only happening every few years. Now that is no longer the case. You may have noticed your nerdiest friends freaking out about the “Vulnerability Apocalypse” this week and waving their arms in panic about something called PHP. You may have also noticed that some of your favorite websites were down for a bit. In the last two weeks of October alone, there have been multiple, potentially internet-breaking vulnerabilities reported and patched. Many of those vulnerabilities were in the open-source software that is the foundation of the vast majority of the internet. For more detailed information on what happened, and why supporting open-source projects matters, check out our other blog . This is all because frontier AI models, such as those created by OpenAI, Anthropic, and others, have made it incredibly cheap and easy to find previously unknown vulnerabilities (zero-days) in open- and closed-source code. stories.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review – a thrilling airport novel of a game
stories.summary: Activision; PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox From parkour over Manhattan rooftops and car chases in Paris to the climactic battle at a North Korean air base, the developers have thrown absolutely everything at the game And so we return perhaps one final time to Call of Duty’s Modern Warfare strand, with stories, “ripped from the newspaper headlines”, featuring shady terror organisations, nefarious rogue states and the brutally capable, monosyllabic war fighters who stand between us and Armageddon. Last year’s Black Ops 7 instalment was a sales disappointment for Activision, and that has no doubt put extra pressure on Infinity Ward, the studio leading Modern Warfare 4 development. stories.title: Salon owners urge Budget VAT cut as staffing pressures grow
stories.summary: Marcus Perkins, who owns a hair and beauty salon in Brierley Hill, says he is scared for the future.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Marcus Perkins said rising costs were making it harder for salons to employ staff and train apprentices

Published 26 October 2026, 06:14 GMT

After 22 years running a salon, Marcus Perkins says he is increasingly worried about the future of the hair and beauty industry.

Rising costs are making it harder for businesses to employ staff and invest in apprenticeships, he says, while more salons are turning to self-employed models to survive.

"Seeing salons close on the high street is very scary," he said. "I'm very scared myself. Luckily it hasn't happened yet but who knows what the future holds?"

Perkins is among more than 2,000 salon owners who have signed an open letter calling on the Chancellor John Healey to cut VAT on hair and beauty services from 20% to 10% in this week's Budget.

The letter is backed by the British Hair Consortium (BHC), which argues rising business costs are placing increasing pressure on traditional salon employers.

However, the industry has also seen growing numbers of stylists move into self-employed arrangements, with hairdressers often renting a chair within a salon rather than being directly employed.

With salon ownership perceived to be out of reach for many, self-employment offered independence, flexibility and higher earnings, industry research suggested , external .

A Treasury spokesperson said hair and beauty businesses played an important role in supporting jobs, apprenticeships and thriving high streets.

They added that the sector had benefited from reforms to business rates.

While traditional salons said they faced rising pressures, a recent report from the British Beauty Council found that hair and beauty salons and shops made up almost a third of all leisure sites across UK retail centres.

It added that those businesses now accounted for greater share of smaller high streets and were equivalent to pubs, bars and cafes combined.

Stylist Trearna Hart fears fewer salons will be able to train the next generation

There were 50,400 VAT or PAYE registered hair and beauty salons in the UK as of March 2025, according to the Office for National Statistics , external . That compared to 49,300 in March 2024.

Salon owners say they have also been affected by increases in wage, pension and National Insurance (NI) costs.

The government's changes to employers' NI contributions and increases to the minimum wage have been defended by ministers as part of wider efforts to improve pay, support public services and drive economic growth.

The BHC said a reduction in VAT would help businesses take on more staff, invest in training and keep more salons trading on the high street.

What is the Budget and what could be in it? Published 12 hours ago

Chancellor says he will cut 'pointless paperwork' to save businesses up to £800m Published 3 days ago

Perkins believed it would make a significant difference.

"We can grow the business and employ more people," he said.

The salon owner runs M&M Spa in Quarry Bank, near Brierley Hill, where he says he has trained more than a dozen young people over the past two decades.

Among them is 21-year-old stylist Trearna Hart, who said many of her peers had struggled to establish careers after leaving college.

She said she was fortunate to find an employer willing to invest in her development.

Dorothy Senior says visiting her salon is about more than having her hair and nails done

This year alone, Perkins said he had spent about £2,000 on courses and travel costs to support her training.

"It's upsetting really," he said. "We help people, we train, we nurture, we mentor. We help the next generation because if we don't help the next generation, what happens to our future?"

The BHC claimed apprenticeship numbers had fallen sharply and warned the trend could worsen if pressures on employer-run salons continued.

Financial pressures and concerns over inconsistent training standards had led salons to take on fewer apprentices, with 53% of salon owners reporting a reduction , external in the number they trained, according to a Future of Hairdressing report.

Perkins believes businesses that employ and train staff are increasingly competing against models centred on self-employed workers.

He argues that creates an "unlevel playing field" because traditional salons often shoulder the costs of training future hairdressers.

Hart said the number of salons disappearing from high streets was a concern.

"At the rate it's going we're not going to have many salons left open and there's no-one going to be able to do hair," she said.

The challenges facing the sector are also worrying some customers.

Research from the British Beauty Council highlighted the role hair and beauty businesses play in supporting local high streets, encouraging spending and providing opportunities for social connection.

Dorothy Senior has visited M&M for hair and beauty treatments for the past 20 years.

She said the salon was about much more than appearances.

"Every time I come in I go home feeling so much better," she said. "It isn't just having nails and hair done, it's the whole package."

stories.body:
At least 18 million people living in poverty across the Indo-Pacific fish in seagrass meadows, while around 6.5 million rely on them as their only fishing grounds. For these communities, the underwater habitats are not simply part of the natural environment but a source of food and a means of earning a living.

But these important fishing grounds face growing pressure from coastal development, changes in land use and poor water quality. When seagrass meadows are damaged or lost, the consequences can extend beyond wildlife. The fish and other marine life they support may also be affected, putting food supplies and household incomes at risk.

Our latest research examines the scale of this dependence and how it relates to poverty. The findings highlight a question that conservation efforts need to address: what happens to people whose livelihoods depend on habitats that are under growing pressure?

Seagrasses are flowering plants that grow in shallow coastal waters. They form underwater meadows that support fish and other marine life. People can fish in these habitats using simple nets, traps and lines, or collect shellfish and other marine animals by hand. Unlike some other fishing grounds, seagrass meadows can often be reached without a boat or expensive equipment.

This level of accessibility can be particularly important for households with few resources or alternative ways to earn money. Yet seagrass conservation is often discussed in terms of protecting wildlife and storing carbon. We have known that these habitats support fisheries, but we have had much less understanding of how many people living in poverty rely on them.

To investigate this, we analysed data from nearly 2,000 households in more than 150 coastal communities across Cambodia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Sri Lanka and Tanzania.

We looked at household incomes, fishing activities and the habitats people used to catch fish and collect other marine resources. We then compared the livelihoods of households using different fishing grounds, including those living in poverty.

More than 80% of households in the communities we studied were involved in fishing, either to earn money, provide food or both. Households that relied entirely on seagrass fisheries earned around 23% less than those fishing in other habitats, even after we accounted for differences in household size.

To put this in perspective, if a household earns £7.50 per day, a 23% difference amounts to roughly £52 a month. For a family already struggling to afford food, healthcare or education, this is a substantial amount of money.

The dependence was especially striking among households living in extreme poverty. Almost half fished in seagrass as well as other habitats, while more than a 25% relied on seagrass alone. This does not mean that seagrass fishing causes poverty. Rather, accessible fishing grounds may be particularly important to people who cannot afford a boat or specialist equipment.

We then combined our household data with estimates of how many people live near seagrass meadows. Across the five countries we studied, we estimate that 10.8 million people living in poverty use seagrass for fishing. Around 5.4 million may rely on it as their only fishing habitat.

The stakes go beyond income. In separate research published earlier this year, we found that fish communities associated with seagrass could provide a wider range of essential nutrients than those associated with coral reefs. Although reefs supported more fish overall, seagrass fish communities had greater potential to supply several important nutrients together.

These include iron, which helps prevent anaemia, zinc, which supports children’s growth and immune systems, calcium, which is essential for health bones, and omega-3 fatty acids which support brain development. For families that cannot afford a varied diet, fish, even as a soup or broth, can provide several of these nutrients in a single meal. Losing access to seagrass could therefore not only mean losing income, but also a vital source of nutrition, especially for children and vulnerable family members.

These risks are important considerations because seagrass meadows face pressure globally . Research suggests that around 20% of surveyed seagrass meadow area in the Indo-Pacific has been lost over the past 70 to 90 years , with coastal development and declining water quality among the major threats identified.

Elsewhere in the Indo-Pacific, researchers documented an 84% decline in fish abundance following substantial seagrass loss. For coastal families that depend on these habitats, this means fewer fish available to catch, fewer income opportunities and less food.

Protecting seagrass means protecting people

Protecting these habitats, however, is not as simple as restricting fishing. Conservation measures that limit access to fishing grounds could harm communities if they depend on them for food or income and have few alternatives. At the same time, local fishers may have little control over other sources of damage, such as pollution from agriculture or development along the coast.

Read more: Human connections to seagrass meadows date back 180,000 years, study reveals

Conservation plans therefore need to consider both the health of seagrass meadows and the people who depend on them. Where restrictions on fishing are proposed, decision-makers should assess the probable effects on local incomes and food supplies. They should also consider whether realistic alternatives are available and address damage caused by pollution and coastal development, rather than placing the burden of conservation on fishing communities alone.

In the Philippines, local fishing communities are already helping manage marine reserves that protect seagrass meadows . Some approaches allow fishing and shellfish collection to continue while restricting more damaging activities or protecting smaller areas where marine life can recover.

In Indonesia, years of forest clearance had increased soil erosion, washing sediment into coastal waters and threatening seagrass meadows. In response, local governments, communities and organisations came together to plant more than 4,500 trees along riverbanks to reduce the amount of sediment entering the sea and protecting the seagrass fishing grounds that local families depend on.

Protecting seagrass will not solve coastal poverty on its own, however. But our findings show why conservation policies need to recognise the people who depend on these habitats. Safeguarding seagrass means protecting not only marine life but also an important source of food and income for millions of people.
