stories.title: Board of Deputies of British Jews declares Greens to be racist party
stories.summary: The Jewish body's vote comes in response to the Green Party passing a "Zionism is racism" policy motion.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 25 October 2026

The Green Party of England and Wales has been declared a racist organisation by the Board of Deputies of British Jews.

The Jewish body, which is the largest in the UK, was responding to the "Zionism is racism" policy motion passed at the Green Party's conference earlier this month.

Board of Deputies president Phil Rosenberg said a vote passed by 118 votes to one to declare that the Greens had, "by adopting an antisemitic platform, become a racist party".

A spokesman for the Greens insisted the party does not discriminate against people who hold Zionist views and said it rejected the Board of Deputies' "characterisation of this motion and our party".

They added the decision "will not stop us from speaking out against the genocide in Gaza and pushing for stronger sanctions against the Israeli government and its leaders". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.

The motion passed by the Board of Deputies urged other parties not to do deals with the Greens unless they rejected the policy.

Forming coalition deals with Greens at local or national level would be "failing to take antisemitism with the requisite seriousness", it said, unless the party's local leadership have rejected the policy and committed to overturn it.

Labour has already issued an ultimatum to local Green groups it is currently in coalition with, telling them to disown the motion or lose the party's support.

Rosenberg said: "By adopting an antisemitic platform, the Green Party of England and Wales has become a racist party. We will treat it accordingly.

"No political party has the right to tell Jews that a central part of our identity, rooted in thousands of years of history, faith and peoplehood, is racist.

"The Green Party's policy brands much of our community, including our synagogues and communal organisations, with that slur. It gives prejudice against Jews a political licence.

"The Green Party's leadership must now take responsibility for reversing this policy and confronting the antisemitism it has legitimised."

The motion backed by Green members at its party conference earlier this month said Zionism was an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/ or domination of the non-Jewish population".

It was criticised by Jewish groups, as well as four Green MPs and two former leaders, and opposition political parties.

Responding when the Green motion was passed, the Board of Deputies and Jewish Leadership Council said in a joint statement that "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it".

Green Party leader Zack Polanski, who is Jewish, did not take part in the vote on the motion as he left the conference early to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election which was held days later.

He has since told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that, while he would like to make amendments, he would not overturn the motion , which would be party policy until 2028.

stories.body:
We’ve heard much about the end of the west. At the proposed summit between Trump, Putin and Xi, those fears could crystallise

I n the final two years of a US presidency, when Congress has been lost, approval ratings have sunk like a stone and their party has started to think about who’s coming next, the person occupying the Oval Office can feel their power draining away. Domestic legislation, particularly in an era where bipartisan cooperation is almost nonexistent, grinds to a halt. But as the days tick by until the end, and as presidents begin to think about their legacy, there is one part of the job where they still have power: the rest of the world.

In the final weeks of his presidency in 1992 George HW Bush sent 28,000 American troops to Somalia to help end a famine. For Bill Clinton, it was a quixotic attempt to bring peace to the Middle East by ending the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Barack Obama restored diplomatic ties with Cuba, making a historic visit to Havana, as well as a final, successful push on the Iran nuclear deal.

In 10 days, Donald Trump will enter his own twilight zone. He is almost certain to lose control of the House and it’s not impossible he will face a Democratic Senate too. Any hopes of passing domestic policy – not that he’s bothered with that much during his first two years – will disappear. Instead, he will face a series of investigations that could lead, once again, to impeachment.

On the world stage, however, it will be a different story. And unlike Bush senior, Clinton and Obama, his ambitions won’t be peaceful. The first two years of his second term have been catastrophic; the final two could be even worse.

Once the midterms are over, the US is understood to be planning to restart its unwinnable war with Iran , already carrying out exercises with the Israeli military and withdrawing diplomats from the region. Trump’s sellout of Ukraine is well under way. In the past week he has argued that “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine”, while his envoy Steve Witkoff met with Vladimir Putin in Moscow, praising him in a televised meeting as a “humanitarian…and I salute that, I commend you and I thank you again.”

On top of a reckless war in the Middle East and appeasement in Europe, the shadow of a new world order is emerging, which Trump will relentlessly pursue in his final years. Putin has proposed a summit between himself, Trump and China’s Xi Jinping , to be held in China next month.

Such an unprecedented meeting, were it to take place, would have potentially devastating consequences for the rest of us. The three leaders have ambitions to transform the way the world is governed, essentially dividing it into spheres of influence. One summit wouldn’t turn an idea into reality, but it would send us down a very dangerous path. In Europe, it would have an impact beyond Ukraine if the US refused to help protect nations threatened by Russia . In east Asia, the withdrawal of the American security blanket would cause enormous problems for Taiwan, South Korea and Japan, as well as Australia.

We’ve talked a lot about the end of the west over the past two years – this feels like a moment when many of those fears will crystalise.

The Trump administration’s ambition to divide the world into spheres and side with dictators over democrats has long been evident. Last year’s National Security Strategy was deeply critical of the US’s traditional allies in Europe and east Asia. But it was what it didn’t say that was most shocking. Both Russia and China avoided direct criticism. In six paragraphs describing the threat to Taiwan, China was not mentioned once. Elsewhere in the document, China was actually praised as “rich and powerful … us[ing] its wealth and power to its considerable advantage.” The section on Russia’s war in Ukraine failed to mention how it started and did not suggest that Putin should be defeated; instead it focused on how the US could help Europe and Russia mend their relationship. The 33-page document discussed the importance of the US controlling the western hemisphere, but made clear that so long as the US still had economic dominance, it cared little whether other parts of the world are protected. “The affairs of other countries,” it stated, “are our concern only if their activities directly threaten our interests.” For too long, it argued, America’s allies had “suck[ed] us into conflicts and controversies central to their interests but peripheral or irrelevant to our own”.

For Putin, this is a success almost three decades in the making. He has long viewed American support for democracy in eastern Europe and central Asia as “interference” in Russia’s backyard. Now he has a US president who agrees. Trump has also placed Putin on a far higher pedestal than Russia’s economy and its technological prowess deserves.

Xi, too, has welcomed the US’s rhetorical retreat from east Asia, particularly if it allows China greater maritime control in the East China Sea and South China Sea. World opinion on China has dramatically improved as that of the US has slid. As Chrystia Freeland, a former Canadian foreign minister, put it this week, “there has not been a president who has been more beneficial for China than Donald Trump”.

At stake is not merely territorial control. All three governments see the possibility of increasing economic ties. For the US and China, the bigger issues are future control of economic supply chains and technology platforms, while Russia’s fossil fuel resources are also a factor. All three are key players in the next space race, both in terms of commercial and military control. If these three nations begin to work together, at the expense of Europe and the rest of the world, it will fundamentally change the nature of geopolitics. A decade ago, talk of a multipolar world was based around the idea of the US, China and the European Union as the three most powerful blocs. Somehow, Brussels has been replaced by Moscow.

after newsletter promotion

Until now, the rest of the west has – on the whole – tried to muddle through. Nato still exists on paper, G7 and G20 summits may be chaotic but they still take place. Optimists in the Foreign Office point out that Trump turned up to the UN general assembly and his administration is still deeply involved in the UN’s day to day activities.

Mark Carney spoke of a “rupture” and warned the old post-cold war world was not coming back, but despite warm words from Emmanuel Macron, and renewed discussion about how Europe can protect itself without the US, there is still a sense that everyone is waiting for Trump’s time in office to end. A Great Powers summit makes this harder to ignore.

While US presidents seek foreign policy success in their final months, history suggests they rarely find it. Clinton’s Camp David talks collapsed after Ehud Barak and Yasser Arafat were unable to reach an agreement. Bush would argue that his initial intervention in Somalia eased a famine, but it ended in humiliation. A botched raid on a warlord led to the deaths of 18 US soldiers and several hundred Somalis. Obama’s diplomacy in Cuba and Iran succeeded, but were both promptly ripped up by Donald Trump.

Trump will get his photoshoot – and maybe that’s all he wants – but there is no guarantee that this unsavoury troika becomes a permanent geopolitical fixture. Trump’s foreign policy has divided his Maga movement and has shocked traditional conservatives. The Wall Street Journal editorial board described the proposed summit as “arguably the worst idea of the second Trump term”. A President Vance or Rubio might be less willing to throw in their lot with dictators; a President Ossoff or Ocasio-Cortez certainly won’t.

But just because Trump won’t win, doesn’t mean that the US won’t lose. He will be arriving in Shenzhen at the weakest moment in his presidency. An 80-year-old lame duck leader fated to limp towards the finish line unable to pass any legislation and threatened by two chaotic years of investigations into his alleged corruption. Opposite him will be two authoritarian leaders in their early 70s who believe the only thing preventing them from ruling their nations for another two decades is death. Indeed, given their “hot mic” discussions about longevity drugs last year, perhaps they both believe they can rule for even longer.

If it goes ahead, this summit will bring Putin back in from the cold and reiterate Xi’s position as a global leader who cannot be ignored. The image of the three leaders will come to define this era when the rules-based international order was torn apart and a new, uncertain period began to form.

Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

stories.title: Budget to include £1bn for social and affordable housing
stories.summary: The move will take funding for the 10-year programme to more than £40bn.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Chancellor John Healey will present his first Budget on Wednesday

Published 25 October 2026

More than £1bn for social and affordable housing in England will be provided in the Budget, taking funding for the government's 10-year homes programme past £40bn.

Mayors and regional leaders across England are also expected to get greater powers and funding in Wednesday's announcement - with councils helped to borrow money from the government to invest in house-building through preferential interest rates.

It is hoped the plans will give regional leaders more flexibility and authority over investment decisions.

Chancellor John Healey said English cities and regions would get the "right to decide their own future", while Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the plans were about shifting power to those "who know their communities best".

The chancellor will also announce more support for small breweries, with the Treasury saying he wants "to turn the tide for our pint producers".

Fresh support for breweries follows the news that 310 jobs are at risk at Marston's Brewery in Burton-upon-Trent.

The issue was raised again at Prime Minister's Questions earlier this week, after owners Carlsberg Britvic revealed plans to shut down operations at the historic brewing site.

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith has called for Healey to resign if he fails to set out how the UK will spend 3% of the UK's GDP on defence by 2030.

What is the Budget and what could be in it? Published 12 hours ago

Between quick wins and big dreams lies Burnham's biggest test Published 2 days ago

Under the plans for the regions, an initial £285m in transitional seed funding will be allocated by the government next year to support mayors and local leaders - and reduce reliance on "fragmented bidding pots" in Whitehall, the Treasury said.

The government will also confirm that it will work with mayors to design a new £1.5bn borrowing facility from 2028, which would allow them to access capital needed to support local priorities.

The Treasury said this could be put towards new homes, bringing High Streets back to life, or improving transport links.

Healey said: "Mayors and local leaders know what their communities need to grow, which is why we are giving them more money, more power and more capacity to get projects moving, build homes and make the right decisions for their areas."

Areas across the country which are not yet strategic authorities will be able to access a share of the £285m to "unlock projects which will contribute to growth in their areas".

The prime minister said: "I'm calling time on local leaders going cap in hand to Westminster. That is no way to run a country."

Claire Ward, chairwoman of the UK Mayors Network and Labour's East Midlands mayor, said that having the "right powers and resources through increased devolution" would help turn "ambitious plans into reality and deliver real, lasting change" for communities.

Lord Sadiq Khan, Labour's mayor of London, said greater ability to invest could "help unlock transformational infrastructure projects" including the West London Orbital route, the extension of the Bakerloo Underground line and Docklands Light Railway, and the development of Stratford International station.

Departing Treasury entrepreneurship adviser, Alex Depledge, has criticised the government's treatment of start-ups ahead of her last day on Thursday - the day after the Budget.

She told the Sunday Times , external , that start-ups were being treated as a "sideshow" and should not be pushed to the "margins of economic policy".

"Keeping scale-ups on the fringes underestimates the contribution of our greatest companies, and we need to support and develop them on British shores at all costs," she said.

Leading up to the Budget, defence has also remained a key talking point. Healey resigned in June from his role as defence secretary in the previous government over the defence investment plan , which he claimed fell "well short" of what was needed to fund the armed forces.

He had called for defence spending to rise to 3% of the country's GDP by 2030, on the way to reaching a Nato target of 3.5% in 2035.

But urging him to commit to setting out plans to spend 3% of GDP on defence, the shadow chancellor said: "We are living in an era of extraordinary threats, and yet the chancellor is dithering over finding the money to pay the country's insurance premium... you cannot have a strong economy without a strong defence".

Responding to Andrew Griffith's comments, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the Conservatives were to blame for failing to invest in the military while in office.

Streeting said the prime minister had made it clear that his government was "determined to give our armed forces the investment needed to keep us safe".

stories.title: Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm
stories.summary: Scotland editor James Cook finds out what life is like on board a ship in an untapped oil field awaiting its fate.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 25 October 2026

When we landed by helicopter at Rosebank, this oil field was at the centre of a political storm - and set to be in the path of a real one.

We arrived on Wednesday morning, just a few hours after the UK government had granted consent for the production of gas from the Jackdaw field in the North Sea.

But already attention was shifting to this wild and windy patch of the North Atlantic – the next big decision for Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

Rosebank is bigger than Jackdaw, it would generate higher greenhouse gas emissions, and it could be far more lucrative for its owners, Adura and Ithaca.

Nicola Boyd loves her job on the Petrojarl Rosebank vessel

This summer, along with a camera crew, I travelled to Jackdaw, 150 miles east of Aberdeen.

Now we were the first journalists to visit Rosebank.

We came here - days before Storm Boelo arrived with strong winds and heavy rain - to scrutinise a controversial project which is at the heart of a national debate about climate change, energy policy and the economy.

But we also hoped for a rare glimpse into life offshore.

"It's good fun, it's interesting, every day can change," said Nicola Boyd, who runs the helideck, and greeted us as we struggled out of our lifejackets and survival suits.

Boyd has worked offshore for nearly a decade, including a year on Rosebank - where she spends two weeks at a time followed by three weeks' leave.

"It's a job I love," she added.

The Petrojarl Rosebank is moored in the North Atlantic waiting to see if production gets the go-ahead from the UK government

It's also a job that calls for steady legs and a strong stomach.

Unlike the fixed Jackdaw platform, this installation – 80 miles north west of Shetland – is a large ship, a floating production, storage and offloading vessel (FPSO) named the Petrojarl Rosebank.

It's been chartered by the field's owners from Aberdeen-based Altera and, during my 48 hours on board, it was constantly but gently rolling on the North Atlantic swell.

Those conditions may be misleading.

With the understatement typical of an Orkney islander, lead mechanical technician Ewan Leonard told me the winter weather could be "a bit of a challenge."

"Last week we had a 30m heave coming through," he said, referring to the swell, "so we'll probably suffer more of that as the winter goes on."

Altera CEO Chris Brett told me that in the industry the environment west of Shetland is considered "as harsh as you get anywhere in the world."

Whatever your view on that industry, the sheer scale of what humans have achieved in such conditions is impressive.

Ewan Leonard says the winter weather can be "a bit of a challenge"

The deep reserves of skill, ingenuity and engineering prowess among the 122 people on board are obvious.

The jobs are well-paid and, according to Ewan Leonard, the facilities are excellent.

"We have single-man cabins, there's good gym facilities, there's a lot of rec rooms here."

Douglas Hogge, a production supervisor in charge of a team responsible for the safe extraction of oil and gas, agrees.

"There's the gym, the sauna," he said, adding "you can obviously go and get some fresh air. There's plenty of fresh air out there."

There's even a cinema.

Food on board the ship was described as "fantastic"

"As you've seen yourself, the food is fantastic on board, so no complaints." added Leonard.

Everyone we spoke to agreed with that, praising the talented chefs who sent out all sorts of delicious dishes, from braised ox cheek to mackerel to pork loin, day and night.

As dusk gathers and the nightshift get ready for work with a strange breakfast of fillet steak and chocolate brownie pudding, the vessel begins to glow in the gloom.

It is a strange sight, the decks criss-crossed by a bewilderingly complex array of pipes, valves and bright yellow steelwork.

The ship is an array of pipes, valves and bright yellow steelwork

The ship doesn't move far, rotating around a fixed central point called the turret to face into the weather, making life a little easier for those on board.

If production is approved, oil and gas will be pumped up through the turret from wells in the field below, which contains an estimated 300m to 500m barrels, enough for perhaps 25 years.

"For myself and a lot of the guys, that would see us out to retirement," said Douglas Hogge.

"We need to see this approved," he added.

Environmental campaigners strongly disagree. They've been trying to stop Rosebank for years, with some success.

"The future of the energy sector in the UK is renewable energy," said Tessa Khan, executive director of the campaigning group Uplift.

Consent for production at Rosebank was first granted under the Conservative government in 2023.

But in 2025, after a challenge by Greenpeace and Uplift, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled the approvals of the UK's largest known untapped oil field and Jackdaw were unlawful because they had failed to take into account the climate impact of actually burning the fossil fuels in cars, homes and factories.

The judge, Lord Ericht, said the fields' developers could carry on with work short of producing oil and gas while they provided more detailed environmental assessments for the government and regulators to consider.

"We think Rosebank would be a disastrous decision and a terrible deal for ordinary people across this country," said Khan, urging prime minister Andy Burnham to prioritise renewables in his quest to re-industrialise the nation.

"If the government's interested in building investor confidence, giving the green light to a major new oil field is going to do the opposite," she argued.

Whatever happens with Rosebank and Jackdaw, the long-term trend for the industry is clear and it is one of decline.

It's a quarter of a century since oil production peaked and in recent years jobs in oil and gas have been disappearing much faster than they're being created in renewable energy such as wind and solar power.

The timeline of Jackdaw and Rosebank

The oil from Rosebank would be loaded onto tankers via a gigantic hose and nozzle, which looks like the super-sized pump of an enormous floating filling station.

From there it would be sold on the international market and, most likely, taken to continental Europe for refining.

Opponents say that proves the project is of little benefit to the UK and should be rejected.

Supporters argue that's not the case because UK and European energy markets are co-dependent, adding that Rosebank will generate millions in tax for the Treasury.

Neil McCulloch, chief executive of Adura – which owns 80% of Rosebank and is a joint venture between Shell and the Norwegian state energy firm, Equinor – is optimistic.

He points out that Rosebank contains not just oil but gas which would be piped to Shetland and on to the St Fergus terminal in Aberdeenshire, with the potential to heat 500,000 British homes at peak production.

Approval of this project, argues McCulloch, could pave the way for four more Jackdaw-sized gas developments in the waters west of Shetland – Tornado, Tornado East, Tobermory and Suilven.

"We would like to proceed with them," he said.

A surge in fossil fuel production if Rosebank is approved is exactly what campaigners fear.

It would, argues Tessa Khan, exacerbate the deadly and damaging impact of climate change for British teachers, nurses, firefighters and families worried about their children while making "huge profits for companies that are already incredibly profitable".

The oil from Rosebank would be loaded onto tankers via a gigantic hose and nozzle

When it comes to the impending UK government decision – which sources have told BBC News should come before Christmas – there is a strange mood at Rosebank.

The decision in favour of Jackdaw has clearly encouraged many on board but it has also highlighted the jeopardy they are facing.

For now, most workers we spoke to said they were just focusing on the job, with its strange rhythms and unusual restrictions – no ability to pop to the shops, no alcohol, a lot of special occasions missed.

And for some on board, very particular cravings.

For steward Liam Davidson, it is a desire to see his French bulldog, Bailey, at the end of his fortnight on board.

"My wee dog's at the heliport when I arrive," he said, "I do miss her."

It is hoped the decision on Rosebank will be made in the next few weeks

For Nicola Boyd, it's her double bed and a pizza delivery.

"I love seeing the family, but for me, it's the pizza," she told me.

But this time there might be a delay in delivering Boyd herself.

She is coming to the end of her fortnight but, as she helped us into our survival suits, the Met Office issued an amber weather warning for much of Scotland.

For Rosebank, it seems, there are stormy seas ahead, one way or another.

stories.body:
North Korean leader travels over New Yalu River Bridge to meet senior Communist party member

Kim Jong-un has visited China, inaugurating a bridge that connects the two countries and saying he hopes to expand cooperation with his neighbour.

The North Korean leader arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday after crossing the New Yalu River Bridge, according to South Korea’s unification ministry, which handles affairs related to North Korea, and China’s official Xinhua news agency.

He met Wang Huning, a member of the standing committee of China’s Communist party. The pair toured a car factory, and promised to strengthen the bilateral relationship.

Kim said his country “stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand practical cooperation, thereby delivering tangible benefits to the peoples of both countries”, according to Xinhua.

Wang then accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, Xinhua said.

The visit appears to be timed to underscore the strength of Kim’s ties with Beijing ahead of the 25 October anniversary of China’s first major victory in the Korean war, which came days after Chinese troops crossed the Yalu River into North Korea in October 1950.

Japan’s Kyodo news agency said on Saturday that traffic controls had been imposed around the bridge and near a museum about China’s role in the war, and that hotel bookings nearby had been restricted.

Diplomatic sources told the agency the measures were linked to a visit by a senior North Korean official.

The 3km bridge opened in mid-October , 12 years after China finished building it, after being held up by delays on the North Korean side. In early September, North Korea and Russia opened the first road bridge across their own short border, leaving Pyongyang newly linked by road to its main backers.

The trip is Kim’s sixth visit to China and his first since September 2025, when he attended a military parade in Beijing alongside the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. Xi visited Pyongyang in June , his first trip there in seven years.

Relations with South Korea, meanwhile, have deteriorated. Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, has issued about 10 statements criticising Seoul since late September, a frequency South Korea’s unification ministry has called unusual, and has also announced plans to resume loudspeaker broadcasts at the border within days.

Xi will host the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, which has fuelled speculation about a meeting between Kim and Donald Trump.

Reuters reported on Friday , however, that US and South Korean officials see little chance of Kim meeting the US president this year.

stories.title: Students like new tenancy freedoms - but landlords warn of higher rents
stories.summary: The Renters' Rights Act gives greater flexibility to leave a tenancy but the changes have posed challenges for student landlords.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Eddie Lever was able to leave his tenancy more easily because of the Renters' Rights Act

Published 25 October 2026

When the Renters' Rights Act came into force in May it was described as the biggest change for tenants in England in a generation, giving more stability and security to the millions of people who rent from private landlords.

The legislation has also prompted a shake-up of the student rental market, which has posed challenges for landlords as it allows people to leave a tenancy rather than being tied in for the full academic year.

Eddie Lever had finished his first year at the University of Exeter when he decided the course wasn't for him.

The 20-year-old wanted to switch to studying international relations at the University of York but had already organised his house for the upcoming year.

The tenancy was signed and had started.

But because of changes in the Renters' Rights Act, Eddie only had to give two months' notice before he could leave and stop paying rent.

The legislation ended fixed-term tenancies - where renters are tied in to contracts for a specific number of months. For students, previously contracts were generally for the full academic year.

Instead, properties are now rented on a rolling basis, which means tenants pay rent weekly or monthly with no fixed end date.

University-owned halls of residence and Purpose-Built Student Accommodation are exempt , external and can still offer fixed-term contracts so this change primarily affects students renting from a private landlord.

"If the Renters' Rights Act wasn't a thing, I don't think I would have been able to move universities because I would have been locked into the full [year] contract," Eddie explains.

"It would have made it unaffordable."

What the Renters' Rights Act means for tenants and landlords Published 30 April

'I fought for change to remove student housing stress' Published 15 November 2025

More students planning to live at home for university over 'insane' living costs Published 22 August

As he was signed up to a joint tenancy, when he left it ended the tenancy for the whole house.

Fortunately, Eddie had a friend who was looking for a room who was able to take his place so his housemates could sign a new tenancy.

He acknowledges the situation would have been more difficult for his housemates if there wasn't someone who could take his room.

However, Eddie thinks the benefits for students are worth this risk.

"If you were to fall out with your flatmates or if you decide that university is not for you, being locked into a full-term contract can be really prohibitive financially," he says.

"So without that flexibility, people can really be locked into situations that they don't necessarily want to be in."

Lewis Wilson, vice president for higher education at the National Union of Students, says this flexibility means students can also save money on rent by moving home for the summer.

While previously, many student rental contracts ran into the summer after courses had finished, students can now choose to move out earlier if they want.

Wilson says students also benefit from wider changes in the act, which bans landlords in England from evicting tenants without a reason.

Campaigners argue this gives renters greater security and confidence to ask for repairs, without fearing they could be evicted if they raise concerns.

Lewis Wilson from the NUS says the legislation has given students more freedom to move out when they want

However, greater flexibility for students to leave tenancies also means less certainty for landlords.

The act did introduce a specific ground , external for landlords to evict a group of students at the end of the academic year if they intend to re-let the property to students.

Chris Norris, chief policy officer at the National Residential Landlords Association, says the bigger problem for student landlords is if their tenants choose to move out earlier.

He argues this is a bigger risk for students - who may fall out with their housemates or drop out of university - than, for example, families, who are less likely to want to move out after just a few months.

Norris says the end of fixed-term tenancies means student houses could be left empty over the summer after courses finish - or even earlier.

He adds that it is now more difficult for student landlords to rent a house for just a few months as they don't know how long the tenants will stay and can't guarantee it will be available for students again in the autumn.

Norris says it's early days for the new legislation and many landlords are taking this year as a test to see how these issues play out in practice.

However, he warns that some may choose to increase the monthly rent they charge to cover the risk of their properties being empty over the summer.

In some cases, he says landlords may even sell up or stop renting to students, reducing supply and pushing up prices.

Sue Lawes thinks the changes mean many student landlords will put up their rent

Sue Lawes, who rents three shared houses to students in Norwich, is worried about the changes.

While Sue says she doesn't want to put up her prices, if her houses end up being empty over the summer because students decide to end their tenancy after their final exams she says she may have to.

She has already brought forward the start of her tenancy agreements to August instead of September to try and reduce the risks of this.

However, she says if her tenants move out earlier in the year she would struggle to make a profit, whilst covering costs including her mortgage, council tax and utility standing charges when the properties are empty.

She argues higher monthly rents would mean bigger upfront costs for students and higher overall costs for those who do choose to carry on renting over the summer.

Sue stresses that she supports the aim of the legislation to give tenants greater security and that students should be able to move out if their landlord is not carrying out repairs.

But she wants landlords to be allowed to offer fixed-term contracts to students in line with the academic year to avoid properties being left empty over the summer.

"Landlords are going to find it very, very hard to absorb those void periods," she says.

"Landlords will put prices up and students are going to pay."

Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan .

Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.

Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.

Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.

Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

Blaming a moribund economy on too many rules is a hackneyed neoliberal trope – UK plc needs smarter regulation, not less regulation

B efore becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham pledged to “end 40 years of neoliberalism”. But as he prepares for his first budget on Wednesday, his government is yet to let go of one of its most tedious cliches: red tape.

In the run-up to the chancellor John Healey’s high-stakes Commons address, the government issued a press release last week promising his plans would include measures to “slash the red tape choking firms”.

Named after the tape once used to tie up government bills, and popularised by the historian Thomas Carlyle, the phrase is straight from the neoliberal playbook and has long outlived its usefulness.

Getting the interfering state out of the way of the wealth creators was a trope of Thatcher and Reaganite economics, and on this side of the pond it has been repeated ad nauseam by every government since.

Thatcher unleashed the City with her “ big bang ” deregulation drive, and her successor John Major was enthusiastic about “hacking back the jungle of red tape”. It was the man he appointed for the job – Michael Heseltine – who coined what has become the most hackneyed description of this particular approach: the “bonfire of red tape”.

With Labour back in power, Gordon Brown celebrated a light-tough regulatory regime for the UK’s hard-driving financial sector – until the Treasury had to bail out the banks after the 2008 financial crisis.

Boris Johnson wanted to unfetter Britain’s businesses from “Brussels bureaucracy” and waffled on during the Brexit campaign about bendy bananas. Yet, after Brexit, business groups said their members would rather comply with longstanding EU standards in many areas than adopt an entirely new UK regime. And bananas are no more or less bendy than before.

Rachel Reeves had a more unpleasantly graphic way of making a similar point, referring to regulation as a “boot on the neck” of British business.

There is nothing wrong with ensuring the interaction between business and the state is smooth. But even during the early years of neoliberalism, the free market good, regulation bad dichotomy was always unhelpful, for several reasons.

First, good regulation – a robust competition regime, for example – is essential to make markets work well. And even most enthusiasts for a laissez-faire approach would acknowledge the need for some basic quality standards – for food and medicines, for example.

When it comes to the labour market, Labour has unashamedly adopted a pro-regulation stance. Its Employment Rights Act is the most significant increase in workers’ rights in a generation – but it inevitably, and deliberately, increases the rules firms must follow.

That is to the benefit, ministers rightly argue, of low-paid employees trapped in insecure work. But a bonfire of red tape it is not. Labour posing as a champion of deregulation will seem unconvincing, given that context.

Second, and ironically, the march of neoliberalism itself is a reason regulation has mushroomed in recent decades. As the Labour MP Yuan Yang argued in a recent lecture for the journal Renewal, as the state retreated from providing important services, watchdog institutions to oversee the private sector became necessary.

As she put it: “The neoliberal illusion, that privatisation liberated markets from state interference, obscures the reality that the state already significantly controls our privatised utilities, but through a maze of arm’s length regulatory agencies which operate outside democratic influence.”

For the water sector, privatised in 1989, these include Ofwat, which sets bills (with the Competition and Markets Authority acting as an appeals body in the event of a dispute); the Drinking Water Inspectorate; the Environment Agency; and the Consumer Council for Water.

Yet, as Yang points out, none are responsible for drawing up a coherent plan for the sector as a whole. “Everyone knows how this story ends: with our rivers polluted and our water infrastructure dangerously lacking.”

after newsletter promotion

Hacking away at the regulatory thicket fails to deal with the structural features of the economy that make the rules necessary in the first place.

Mat Lawrence, the director of the thinktank Common Wealth and author of The Productive State, a policy paper influential among those close to Burnham, calls this “the regulatory state”. He cites affordable housing targets for private developers as another example of regulation taking the place of stuff the state once did itself.

The third reason the endless red tape discourse is unhelpful is one raised by Mike Clancy, the general secretary of the Prospect union, which represents workers at many of the regulators.

He has urged the government to lay off these often not lavishly paid staff, who are trying to do their jobs with stretched resources. “Regulators continue to be labelled as ‘blockers’ despite the vital work they do keeping us safe and protecting our natural environment,” he said.

Prospect has been urging the government to ditch a promise to “cut the administrative burden” of regulation by 25% by the end of the parliament, arguing it is arbitrary and potentially counterproductive.

Finally, we would all benefit from some over-mighty businesses being reined in by regulation, not least the tech firms, which insouciantly concede that their AI agents have been busting through safety controls and may be about to start spawning spontaneously .

Embracing the tired idea that red tape is “choking” business is hardly likely to help the government make the case for the more stringent approach that is clearly necessary.

As it happens, Bonfire Night is almost upon us. If Burnham really wants to embrace a different approach to the economy, he could start by consigning the phrase “red tape” to the flames.

Kim Jong-un has opened the borders to both his key allies in Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, but for different reasons

For more than a decade, local Chinese residents pilloried it as nothing more than an empty bridge that led to a North Korean vegetable patch on the other side.

Fast forward 12 years and dozens of trucks are now traversing the bridge linking China to North Korea, boosting trade for the reclusive regime. But it has also triggered concern that it could intensify a struggle for influence over the North between Beijing and the region’s other major power, Russia.

The New Yalu River Bridge connects the north-eastern Chinese city of Dandong with Sinuiju in North Korea and has four lanes and stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu river. It is expected to ease congestion on the ageing Friendship Bridge nearby.

It opened on 15 October, about a month after another major crossing – this time between North Korea and Russia. The first road bridge across their short shared border , named the Yakov Novichenko Bridge, reportedly made Chinese officials uneasy, coming on top of signs from the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un that he is prioritising ties with Moscow.

“China’s interest in buttressing its influence in North Korea is certainly reinforced by the diversifying North Korea-Russia relationship — ties that China tolerates but watches closely as they add complexity to its relationship with its provocative neighbour,” says Carla Freeman, director of the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies’ Foreign Policy Institute.

Since late 2024, the North Korean leader has sent ammunition and as many as 16,000 troops to support Vladimir Putin ’s war in Ukraine, and has held two summits with the Russian president in the past three years. In 2024, the leaders signed a mutual defence pact that includes a clause requiring the countries to come to each other’s aid if attacked.

In return for arms and combat soldiers, Pyongyang is getting hard currency, real-time battlefield experience for its troops, weapons technology and the opportunity to extend political and economic cooperation beyond its traditional ally China .

North Korea stands to benefit from increased trade but for China, the bridge could be of more geopolitical value than economic given how little trade China does with its neighbour compared with its other partners.

However, the insular regime in Pyongyang is thought to be reluctant to increase its economic dependence on China, by far its biggest trading partner and aid donor, and may still resent Beijing’s previous support for UN sanctions targeting the North’s nuclear weapons programme .

In the past two years, however, Russian and Chinese support for UN sanctions has collapsed. “The main restriction on trade with North Korea is not the infrastructure but international sanctions,” says Justin Hastings, a professor of international relations and comparative politics at Sydney University. “However, because China’s enforcement of UN sanctions has become desultory and Russia has actively repudiated their enforcement, North Korea is in a position to benefit from increased trade and weapons help (at least from Russia).”

The North’s “open” border with China contrasts dramatically with the one it shares with South Korea. In 2024, the North said it would sever all rail and road links with its neighbour, months after Kim said he would abandon the goal of peaceful reunification and declared South Korea his country’s “ principal enemy ”.

But Fyodor Tertitskiy, a North Korea expert at Korea University in Seoul, believes neither China nor Russia can influence North Korea in any meaningful way, citing Kim’s refusal to surrender his nuclear weapons or moderate his iron grip on power – two changes that would be welcomed in Moscow and Beijing.

“Both countries understand that Kim Jong-un would rather accept a complete breakdown in relationships than submit,” he says. “So I doubt we are seeing a straightforward struggle for influence. Kim is trying to play the two against each other, but China and Russia are not rivals like the Soviet Union and China were in the 1970s.”

Kim is more likely to turn to China improve his country’s struggling economy, while Beijing is eager to revive its role as the North’s biggest influence, according to Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.

“After expanding military cooperation with Russia … Kim Jong-un is leveraging his windfall from Moscow for additional gains from Beijing. China may seek to recover lost influence by increasing trade and people-to-people exchanges, but the Kim regime prizes autonomy and wants to limit foreign ideological and cultural influences.”

The South Korean government said last year that at least 17 active road and rail links connect North Korea and China along their 1,400 km-long border.

Tertitskiy is “not particularly optimistic” that the increased contact the bridges will bring means improvements to the lives of ordinary North Koreans or lead to a more western-style economy. “I think it will make reform even less likely. Why pursue reforms and take risks when you can just get what you need from abroad?”

Analysts say the expected rise in trade across the Yalu bridge is likely to be modest at first. But it could become a bellwether for the state of Sino-North Korean ties, says Easley.

“China remains economically indispensable to North Korea in ways that Russia cannot replace,” he says, adding, “In that sense, the bridge may offer an inadvertent window into bilateral relations if flows are visibly interrupted in the future.”

stories.summary: Data centres are the lifeblood of our digital world, but there are growing concerns about their environmental impact. The BBC explores their rise in charts.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing

Published 25 October 2026

Until a few years ago many of us may have been blissfully unaware of what a data centre was.

These giant, warehouse-like buildings power virtually all our internet activity, from our web searches and emails to movie downloads and online banking.

They are at the heart of the AI boom, housing the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run services like ChatGPT and Claude.

But the speed at which they're growing, the enormous amount of electricity they consume and concerns about their environmental impact are fuelling a public backlash around the world.

In the US, they've become a huge issue ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, with both Republicans and opposition Democrats coming out against their development.

It's putting opponents of data centre expansion on a collision course with US President Donald Trump, who has dismissed the pushback as a "sick conspiracy", even as public anger grows.

Here's what you need to know about the data centre boom, and why opposition is growing.

They are growing rapidly

There are about 12,250 data centres around the world, according to Data Center Map , external , a company that tracks both operational and pre-operational sites.

That's up sharply from 2021, when there were around 8,000 , external operational sites.

As the chart below shows, data centres are most densely clustered in the US which has 4,767 sites. It is followed by Europe, where the UK and Germany lead.

Data centres have typically been located near to cities where it's easier to access high voltage power lines or water resources for cooling. But as they get bigger, more are being built in rural areas.

But when it comes to actual capacity, the US is ahead by a much larger margin, with China in second place and Europe lagging far behind.

This gap is set to widen in the coming years, leading some to warn Europe risks missing out on the potential economic benefits of the AI boom , external .

They are getting bigger

Data centres vary wildly in size, ranging from ones that fit inside a garden shed to others covering vast expanses of land.

The world's largest operational data centre is widely reported to be one run by China Telecom in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, covering an area of approximately one million square metres (10.7 million sq ft). That is equivalent to about 140 Fifa football pitches.

However, much larger sites are under construction as the graphic below shows.

All these sites are being built exclusively to provide the immense computing power needed to run AI services.

For instance, Colossus 2, which is part of the wider Colossus campus, will house hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips made by tech giant Nvidia.

It will also be used to train xAI's chatbot Grok. Elon Musk's company will use 41 methane gas turbines to help power the site, which activists say could "significantly increase" local air pollution , external . Local regulators say the turbines will meet air quality standards.

They use more electricity than France

The pressure data centres put on local resources has sparked increasing concern. These facilities can use significant amounts of water to cool their systems, which could lead to water shortages , some experts say.

Data centres worldwide are also thought to consume more electricity than the whole of France, as the chart below shows.

This growing hunger for power is driving up carbon emissions, analysis shows , while putting pressure on local grids, which some fear could push up energy prices .

With others worried about the noise data centres make and the space they take up, a public backlash is gathering steam.

Some 16 US states have proposed laws to ban or temporarily block new facilities, and it could be a key issue in November's midterm elections .

Outside the US, opposition to data centres has emerged in countries like Mexico , France, Indonesia and the UK .

But they can boost jobs

But supporters say data centres are critical to national security , and the development of AI.

They also say they are good for the economy , external , attracting investment, generating tax revenue and creating jobs in areas like construction.

A recent report by the Brookings Center , external suggests data centres do create local jobs, although fewer than industry advocates claim.

The type of data centre matters too. So-called hyperscale facilities - massive sites owned and run by tech giants like Amazon and Microsoft - have a bigger positive effect on jobs, it found.

But "colocation" facilities, which lease space to remote tenants without a local presence, brought fewer benefits.

As the debate over their merits intensifies, the data centre rollout continues.

This year, the tech industry is expected to spend a combined $765bn , external ($544bn) on AI infrastructure in 2026, with this topping $1tn next year.

But as concerns about the environmental impact grow, the tech industry is exploring alternatives.

One idea is to put data centres in space , external or on the Moon , where they could harness abundant solar energy.

Others predict that more AI processing could eventually be carried out by the hardware already inside our computers and smartphones , reducing the need for vast data centres altogether.

stories.title: Between quick wins and big dreams lies Burnham's biggest test
stories.summary: The prime minister might be dreaming of gold medals in 2040, but he must first navigate the difficult years in between, writes Laura Kuenssberg.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Between quick wins and big dreams lies Burnham's biggest test

Published 24 October 2026

Giving the north of England a crack at hosting the globe's biggest sports event might seem about as Brand Burnham as it gets.

Seven million pounds of taxpayers' cash is a teeny drop in the context of the overall Budget, to pay for the government to take a closer look at possible plans. But the idea is sure to get tongues wagging - and headline writers scribbling.

A "Northern Games" in 2040 or beyond just might create a massive sense of national feel-good, jobs and development, as the Olympics in east London did more than a decade ago.

But it's a promise of a possibility at least a decade away. And what could be more in tune with the Manchester-loving prime minister and his proud Yorkshireman chancellor than a sporting plan fixed firmly on the top geographical chunk of the country?

Plan for Northern Olympics to get £7m in Healey's Budget Published 1 day ago

It's Brand Burnham alright, popular with most of the Labour backbenches, just add the Twiglets and the pint in the stands.

The prime minister and his team are proud of a distinct feature of their government so far, focusing on small things that might make a big difference: fines for blaring out music on your phone on the bus, cracking down on "rip-off" parking charges, investing a small amount of cash in a big ambition for a sporting event in future.

It's what some ministers call "the politics of trying" – putting time and effort into ideas that you don't pretend are revolutionary, but give direction, and a sense of sympathy to the public.

It's an echo, deliberate or not, of another Labour Prime Minister, Harold Wilson, who sent memos to his cabinet in 1974 demanding "little things that mean a lot".

He ended up with a list of plans including nationalising small breweries to stop them being gulped up by big firms (paging Andy Burnham), freezing phone installation charges for pensioners, and plans for empty office blocks.

But the next few days could bring an end to that "politics of trying" phase, with one senior official describing the coming Budget as "the first proper moment for the government, which will then be in the pipeline for the 10-year plan, then a very difficult spending review".

What is the Budget and what could be in it?

An influential Labour MP told me: "The Budget has to be the beginning of the future story."

A fancy way of saying, beyond the short-term announcements and clear long-term aspirations, what is this government actually going to do?

"Steady as she goes," is what one well-connected senior MP predicts, and how expectations of the Budget are being managed across Westminster. They tell me: "Not doing a lot might be more reassuring to people than promising the earth with whose money?"

The boss of one well-known high street business told me they are even hoping there won't be any big bazookas. "Just do no harm," they implored the Chancellor John Healey.

"The hole is too big that they are trying to fill, so my view is don't try and do anything big to help because you don't have the money, but don't do anything to harm us either."

After all, the chancellor is bound by Labour's manifesto promises not to fiddle with the main taxes – income tax, VAT, National Insurance for workers. And you don't need me to remind you that public spending, borrowing and tax are all at historic highs.

Chuck in prices jacking up again because of war in the Middle East and there isn't much money to spray around. In fact, some big cuts to public spending are already pencilled in for the later years of this parliament.

The chancellor and prime minister face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households and meet commitments on defence spending

But the widespread suggestion that you'll be able to blink and miss the Budget has got some hackles up in the Treasury. A budget, by its very nature, can never be a small event - it sets billions upon billions of taxes and spending decisions.

And there are likely to be extra taxes on banks, vows to sweep away some business regulation, particularly for small business, more powers passing to local leaders under the guise of devolution and more action on energy bills which are heading back up again.

John Healey has made it clear publicly and to staff, that he wants to encourage people with the guts and drive to start a business. One source said: "If you are taking on John's mantra about talking up Britain then you can't say, 'Nothing to see here'."

Whatever else the chancellor brings to Parliament in his red box, do not expect him to arrive with all the solutions to the country's very well-documented problems, whether that's getting the economy growing more convincingly, sorting out gaps in defence cash, welfare, social care, or new ways to pay off the country's groaning debts more quickly.

One former minister suggests even if Healey and Burnham had stumbled upon all the answers in a few months, it's just not possible to fix everything at the same time because of the constraints on the economy.

They wondered: "Is he going to invest in growth? Is he going to put everything he has into the challenges people will face this winter? Is he going to throw it at defence? There is just not enough to tackle all these problems simultaneously - ministers are going to be exposed to the cold light of day."

Burnham and Healey have to find a way of maintaining the balance in an unusually happy Labour Party.

MPs talk of ministers and Burnham himself being more visible and approachable in Parliament, knocking around with colleagues in the evening, fewer "golden slips" doled out when ministers were excused from voting alongside colleagues so they could get on with their important jobs.

One minister told me they'd had to tell their private office not to arrange for them to be "slipped" , from going to the Commons in the evening to see backbenchers.

It's paying off in the mood among MPs. One told me: "You're not feeling like the only way you can ever have a chat with a minister is by arranging an appointment for three months down the line – the soft touches really matter."

Chancellor John Healey will set out Labour's tax and spending plans when he delivers his first Budget on 28 October

A party that feels the boss has their back is more likely to be receptive to hard decisions, that's simple psychology, and guess what? Politicians are humans too.

But the equilibrium is fragile. One source involved in the Budget prep told me the government "is like a seesaw".

"It's John and James on the right (Healey and Purnell, Burnham's chief of staff), Lou (Haigh) on the left, and Andy balancing it in the middle," adding that "Andy is not as on the left as many of his supporters want to believe".

That balance could be more strained in the coming weeks as choices over immigration and welfare reform loom after the Budget. And how the numbers stack up on Wednesday matters intensely too.

The Labour left will be looking keenly to see if people who are really struggling financially receive meaningful support.

Those on the right will be scouring the statement for measures that display a tight control on spending and help businesses grow. Even small moves could upset the seesaw.

One former minister doubts there will be anything major enough to upset the delicate balance, not because of an abundance of caution but they suggest, "John has been struggling a bit - he hasn't gone into this with a philosophical direction".

There is also a risk that by deferring big decisions until the Spending Review next year - which sets out longer-term spending than an annual budget - it looks like the government is just putting off the hard stuff.

Another acknowledges the danger of looking like it's a budget on the never-never, delaying decisions on "welfare, defence and social care – Andy goes in with political stock quite high – he needs to spend it on difficult stuff and there isn't much sign of it yet".

In an interview with The Times, Andy Haldane, a former chief economist at the Bank of England and an ally of Burnham, said he feared the government would deliver a "mañana budget" that deferred difficult decisions on public spending and "doesn't speak to the urgency of now".

With friends like these…

The former mayor of Greater Manchester became the UK's fourth prime minister in five years and the seventh since 2016

It's a good bet that the opposition parties will pile in on this angle, accusing Healey and Burnham of ignoring the long-term pressures next week. One prominent opposition politician said: "This Budget can only be postponing, you have to assume that's cynical because you are going to have an early election, or you are storing up a car crash for next year (the Spending Review)."

Downing Street sources counter that argument with Burnham's decision to unpick the expensive triple lock to pay, at least in part, for future social care. Or his bolder approach to potentially ask to re-enter the EU, or certainly pursue much closer ties.

And remember that list of small things that could make a big difference? They have made political decisions that the polls suggest voters have noticed.

Even some of Burnham's backers admit quietly that he is aware his first job in office was clear: to show action, to cheer up his party, and that seems to have had a positive effect in the polls.

His long-term view of the UK he wants is well known – with devolution, a national care service, and greater public involvement in the economy.

But the middle bit?

One official says: "Unless the prime minister has said something quite specific about something everyone is scrambling around trying to work out what he wants to do."

Another well-connected source says: "The challenge has always been with this project, how do people feel in the medium term – it's huge."

​​Burnham and his chancellor's start in office has been broadly successful if you look at the polling, or read the mood inside the Labour party.

Their dreams of future glories, long-term plans and policies, and gold medals on UK soil could point ahead to many years time.

But neither deal with the issues that need to be confronted in the middle.

The chancellor was working late in his Downing Street flat last night, finishing off his plans after having fish pie for tea, conscious his first Budget starts the between times - and they're almost here.

stories.title: Wales plans to ban steel pylons as government launches consultation
stories.summary: The Welsh government says it is consulting on an "undergrounding-first approach" to electricity lines.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Building pylons in Wales could be a thing of the past, with the country's ministers instead wanting to bury energy cables underground

Published 23 October 2026

The Welsh government has announced plans to ban the use of traditional steel pylons to support electricity lines over which it has control.

Plaid Cymru ministers favour burying cables underground instead.

Plans for a network of pylons in the Towy Valley have faced a fierce local backlash with local Plaid politicians speaking out against the proposals.

The company behind the plans, Green Gen Cymru, said it welcomed the consultation and that it supported using "the right infrastructure in the right place".

Prohibiting the use of large steel lattice pylons for new lines up to 132 kilovolts was a Plaid Cymru manifesto pledge before May's Senedd election.

Launching a consultation on its policy on Friday, the Welsh government said undergrounding electricity circuits could "reduce the visual impact of electricity infrastructure, helping to protect landscapes and local amenity".

It also said that burying cables could make them less vulnerable to severe weather and could reduce the potential impact on birds and other wildlife.

However, the consultation document also acknowledges that undergrounding was "generally considered more expensive to install and maintain and could create construction impacts during installation".

The government's policy would allow for wooden poles or "equivalent, less intrusive infrastructure" to be used to support overhead cables where undergrounding isn't feasible.

Farmers 'vindicated' after judge's ruling on pylon firm accessing land Published 6 July

Energy firm unveils new slimline pylons designed 'with Welsh landscape in mind' after backlash Published 17 September

Green Gen has plans to build three major power line routes connecting onshore wind farms planned by its sister company Bute Energy with the wider grid network.

It has previously said it would invest nearly £1bn by 2030, with proposals affecting parts of Carmarthenshire, Ceredigion, Powys and Shropshire.

But it has faced considerable opposition in certain communities, with groups representing hundreds of landowners taking the company to court in 2025 .

In a bid to address concerns, Green Gen recently unveiled a "slim and compact" 22 metre (72ft) pylon, designed "with the Welsh landscape in mind".

The company has consistently said that undergrounding its cables would cost on average 4.5 times more , external than running them overhead.

That would mean an extra cost of £500m for the Towy Usk project between Carmarthenshire and Powys, according to Green Gen.

Green Gen Cymru has proposed three pylon routes from mid Wales across to Shropshire, south-west Wales to Ceredigion, and one from the same point to Powys

Eirian Edwards, a campaigner in the Llandovery Pylon Group, said: "We welcome that they are seriously looking at undergrounding as the preferred option - to protect landscapes and people's livelihoods.

"If infrastructure has to be planned, then we're not against that process at all. We realise that we need to strengthen our local grid, but certain projects that are planned do not fulfil that at all."

Dyfan Walters, a farmer in Llandovery who is also a member of Llandovery Pylon Group, called it "a positive day for us".

"We're fully supportive and understand that the infrastructure is required.

"Putting that underground means that there's less impact on agriculture, less impact on tourism.

"In a world where there's an ever-changing climate, having that resilience - having infrastructure placed underground - is a sensible way forward."

Dyfan Walters called it a "positive day" for campaigners

Welsh Energy Minister Adam Price said: "We know the necessary changes in the way energy is generated and used in Wales will require new grid infrastructure, however, we also know that new infrastructure can impact on the communities and the environment that hosts it.

"We want to see infrastructure that is sensitively designed to minimise impacts on the environment and the communities that host them, while offering the maximum benefits for Wales."

Andrew Hardcastle, executive director at Green Gen Cymru, said: "We welcome the Welsh government's consultation and its recognition of the importance of delivering the electricity infrastructure Wales needs in a way that is sensitive to our landscapes, environment and communities.

"Like all grid companies across the UK, we believe there is no one-size-fits-all solution to developing new electricity networks.

"Our approach is to use the right infrastructure in the right place, drawing on a range of technologies including underground cables, wooden poles and our recently announced lower-profile monopoles."

The company said it was "pleased that the consultation recognises the potential role of less visually intrusive overhead infrastructure, including monopoles, and invites evidence on their use".

Reform's Senedd spokesperson for rural affairs, Laura Anne Jones, said: "As part of our energy policy, we will continue to push for new power lines to be placed underground wherever possible, protecting our landscapes and rural communities.

"Reform will always stand up for our countryside and fight against its industrialisation."

Welsh Labour's environment, rural affairs, energy and transport spokesperson, Vikki Howells said: "Burying cables can cost five times as much as overhead lines, making electric more expensive and decarbonisation more difficult."

She said the sensible position was choosing the right engineering solution for the right landscape and "undergrounding should absolutely remain available where landscape, environmental or other circumstances justify it".

The Welsh Conservatives welcomed the policy consultation.

The party's environment spokesperson, Andrew RT Davies said: "We recognise that Wales needs a modern electricity network to support economic growth, but communities should not have to accept eyesores across our beautiful natural landscapes, which must be conserved."

The consultation , external will run until 15 January 2027.
